sections.title: The golden minute: what it is and why it matters

read.text: Contents:

• 1. Goals
  • 2. Introduction: Background and Definitions
  • 3. Importance
  • 4. Before the Golden Minute of life
  • 5. Delayed Cord Clamping (DCC)
  • 6. Thermoregulation and Prevention of Hypothermia
  • 7. Neonatal Resuscitation Initial steps
  • 8. Support of Respiration
  • 9. Support of the Cardiovascular System
Goals

• 1. To understand the concept of the Golden Minute
  • 2. To know the significance of Golden Minute interventions
  • 3. To develop a timely managed approach
  • 4. To be prepared for the sequence of Neonatal resucucition and minimize staff distress
  • 5. To actively participate in minimizing morbidity and mortality associated with delayed resuscitation
Introduction to Golden Minute:
Background and Definitions of Golden Minutes

The first Golden Minute after birth has been identified as a critical window for establishing ventilation in a newborn. That is, if ventilations or chest compressions are required, they are initiated within one minute following delivery; however, do not wait one minute to calculate the APGAR score and then determine that there is a need for resuscitation.
The Golden Minute timeframe starts when the whole body is delivered. The Golden Minute approach focuses on the active intervention during the first minute of life.

Neonatal resuscitators in a variety of settings use the International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation (ILCOR) algorithm to guide delivery room management, including countries implementing the Helping Babies Breathe (HBB) program, which provides resuscitation training and standardized guidelines to medical teams in low-resource settings. Algorithms such as the Neonatal Resuscitation Program apply the same timeline.
Of note, the Golden Minute concept is not restricted to establishing ventilation. It would also involve:

• 1. Readiness for resuscitation
  • 2. Proper initial assessment
  • 3. Thermoregulation and prevention of hypothermia
  • 4. Management of the umbilical cord
Importance of golden minutes:

• 1. Well-arranged Golden Minute interventions facilitate the smooth transition from the cocooned fetal life to the independent neonatal and later adult life
  • 2. Timely planned intervention, as recommended in the first minute of life, would help to minimize serious morbidity such as CP and poor neurodevelopmental outcomes, as well as mortality
  • 3. Lack of knowledge and skills that may be needed or indicated in the first minute of life may affect further resuscitation and outcomes
When does the Golden Minute start?
options: When the whole body of the baby is delivered
One minute after birth, once the APGAR score is calculated
read.explanation: The manual: "The Golden Minute timeframe starts when the whole body is delivered." Do not wait one minute to calculate the APGAR score before deciding the baby needs resuscitation.

sections.title: Antenatal counselling: why and who

read.text: Effective Communication

• 1. Communication with parents ( antenatal counseling
  • 2. Communication with labour and delivery room team.
Antenatal counseling and team briefing
Background:

• 1. The importance of antenatal counseling has been emphasized in neonatal resuscitation program (NRP). The parents should be counseled antenatally, answering all the question asked by them about the newborn thus allaying there anxiety. This hold true for both pre-term and term neonate. If the newborn is going to be shifted to mother side then parents need to be counseled regarding breast feeding and general newborn care
  • 2. The parents should be given appropriate time for making decision over the neonatal management.
  • 3. Evidence shows that rational, consensus peri- viability ( see section 7) guidelines are well accepted and can be used for antenatal counseling by neonatologists, obstetricians, and nurses who provide care to pregnant women and infants at extremely low gestational ages.
  • 4. Ideally both obstetrics team and neonatal team should do counseling together and present a consistent approach for the newborn as this leads to better rapport between neonatologist, obstetrician and parents.
Why should the parents be counseled?
Infants born at an extremely low gestational age have a high mortality rate and are at risk of having neurodevelopmental disabilities ranging from subtle to severe in grade
What is the goal of antenatal counselling?
The goal of antenatal counseling is 1. to inform parents and assist them in decision- making over either providing resuscitation or giving only comfort care to the neonate.
• 2. To prepare parents fir the hospital course and outline management plan if full support was the decision.
Who should ideally do the antenatal counselling?
options: The obstetric team and the neonatal team together
The neonatal team only, after birth
Whoever is free on the ward
read.explanation: The manual: "Ideally both obstetrics team and neonatal team should do counseling together and present a consistent approach for the newborn."

sections.title: Antenatal counselling: basis, components and what to tell parents

read.text: What is the basis for antenatal counseling?

• 1. Estimated gestational age of delivery has shown strong association with neurodevelopmental outcome and it serves as the basis for antenatal counseling.
  • 2. The decision to provide comfort care will also depend upon other variables such as
  • a) the presence or absence of chorioamnionitis, and
  • b) the level of care available for location of delivery ( unite level, presence of specific guidelines. DNR policy ).
  • c) Presence of other complications such as major congenital anomalies.
What are the three components of effective counseling?
The three components of effective counseling are

• 1. assessment of risks,
  • 2. communication of those risks,
  • 3. ongoing support.

read.title: The three components of effective counselling

read.text: What are the benefits of parental counseling?
Antenatal counseling especially before a preterm delivery has many benefits for parent’s like

• 1. reducing parental anxiety,
  • 2. increasing knowledge,
  • 3. facilitating informed decision-making and
  • 4. making rapport with the neonatal clinicians
What are the most important points or issues need to be told and discussed with parents antenatal?

• 1. parents should be told about most accurate prognostic morbidity and mortality data available for their infant based on hospital-specific database or regional or national data. .
  • 2. Parents also need to be informed that inspite to the best efforts, both things namely the exact prognosis or outcome for a specific infant either antenatally or immediately after delivery and prediction of long-term neurologic outcome remains limited.
  • 3. The parents should also be told about expected duration of neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) stay and morbidities which the newborn is likely to face in the postnatal life depending upon the gestational age and birth weight. (The prediction of hospital stay duration will depend upon the gestational age at birth, expected morbidities and previous database of the hospital for the same gestational age neonate.).
  • 4. Documentation:
A mother in preterm labour asks you how long her baby will stay in the NICU. What does the manual say parents should be told before the birth?
read.answer: The most accurate prognostic morbidity and mortality data available (hospital, regional or national); that the exact prognosis and long-term neurologic outcome cannot be predicted exactly; and the expected duration of NICU stay and the morbidities likely for the gestational age and birth weight. The counselling is documented.

sections.title: Calling the neonatal team: the SBAR format

read.text: What are the factors to be considered during counseling parents antenatally for extreme preterm delivery?

The pregnancy outcome will depend upon the birth weight, gestational age, gender, use of prenatal steroids, singleton pregnancy, maternal age, maternal health, maternal nutrition, substance use, genetics, and complications during pregnancy.
Communication with labour and delivery team: high risk deliveries

• 1. Labour ward staff have primary responsibility for assessing the degree of risk anticipated and communicating their concerns effectively to the neonatal team. The earlier the neonatal team is given notice of a potential problem the better, allowing decisions to be made around the appropriate staffing and management at delivery.
If in doubt, call and discuss

• 2. In turn the neonatal team should make every effort to attend promptly and ensure that they have adequate information to make management decisions
  • 3. Communication around an emerging situation where there may be both neonatal and maternal concerns is a challenge, however every effort should be made to ensure that adequate information is accurately passed to the neonatal team when they are called for resuscitation. Ideally the call should be made by a member of staff with a good working knowledge of the situation- if the midwife looking after the mother or midwife in charge is not able to make the call to the neonatal team, they should ensure that when delegating this adequate information is passed on
SBAR format
When calling for neonatal assistance, the SBAR format should be used:

SSituation e.g. - I’ve got a baby about to deliver with meconium and a non reassuring CTG
BBackground e.g. - The baby is at term, mum has gestational diabetes, and there have been no other concerns in pregnancy. The obstetric registar is setting up for a vacuum extraction in the room
AAssessment e.g. The CTG trace is concerning, with late dips ( late decelerations )
RRecommendation e.g. I need you to come to room 4 straight away- will you need the registrar too?
Sort each part of this call from the labour ward into its SBAR heading.

read.text: Communication with obstetrical team
• 1. Identification of maternal, fetal and intrapartum factors.
The NRP guidelines recommend that resuscitation team to ask the obstetrician 4 questions to identify maternal, fetal risk that may predict the need for resuscitation: (see box below)

• Q (1) What is the expected gestational age?
  • Q (2) Is the amniotic fluid clear?
  • Q (3) Are there any additional risk factors?
  • Q (4) What is our umbilical cord management plan?
The 3 rapid questions:
Those neonates who do not require resuscitation can generally be identified by a rapid assessment using 3 questions.

• 2. Is this a term gestation?
  • 3. Does the neonate have good muscle tone?
  • 4. Is the neonate crying or breathing?
If the answer to all 3 of these questions is “yes,” the neonate does not need resuscitation and can stay with the mother for routine care.
A baby is born at term, with good muscle tone, crying. What do the 3 rapid questions tell you?
read.answer: All three answers are "yes" (term, good tone, crying or breathing), so the neonate does not need resuscitation and can stay with the mother for routine care.

sections.title: Equipment checks and preparation for specific conditions

read.text: Equipment checks and preparation:

• NRP recommends prior preparation of standardized equipment kits to save time in an emergency.
  • Each unit should have its standard equipment list (see below) and standard checklist (see below).
  • The equipment list may vary according to unit facility and level; however, NRP equipment should be standardized.
  • Newborn resuscitation equipment should be checked routinely and frequently on a daily basis or periodically during the day and after use.
  • A team member should be assigned for a routine check-up.
  • The prior resuscitation equipment check should be done with each call, even if the routine checkup has been done.
  • The prior resuscitation equipment check must be done quickly and in a systematic way.
  • Double-check or confirmation by a senior member of the team is recommended if there is enough time.
The routine daily equipment check was done this morning. A call comes for a delivery. Do you check the equipment again?
options: Yes: the prior resuscitation equipment check is done with each call, quickly and systematically
No: the routine check this morning is enough
Only if the baby is preterm
Only if a senior asks for it
read.explanation: The manual: "The prior resuscitation equipment check should be done with each call, even if the routine checkup has been done."

read.text: Appropriate area for resuscitation of the newborn

• Infant resuscitator with in-built heater and light, or a firm, padded resuscitation surface and an overhead warmer.
  • Clock with a timer in seconds
  • Good light in the resuscitation area.
  • Appropriate personal protective equipment (PPE) according to the level of risk
  • Temperature maintenance:
    • Warmed towels or warm wraps
    • Polyethylene bag or sheet for infants less than 32 weeks’ gestation or less than 1500 grams’ birth weight
    • Woolen hats (various sizes)

PRACTISE THIS SKILL Preparation for specific neonatal conditions
Preterm infant <32 weeks’ gestation or less than 1500 grams:
• Prepare a polyethylene bag or sheet/wrap.
• If using a polyethylene bag: cut a square hole (large enough for the infant’s head) into the end opposite the zip lock.
• At birth, the infant’s body (but not the head) should be placed immediately into the bag or wrap (wet and warm) and directly under a radiant heat source.
• The infant’s head should be dried, and a woolen hat placed onto the infant’s head
A baby is born at 30 weeks. How is the polyethylene bag used?
options: The body (not the head) goes into the bag wet, under a radiant heat source; the head is dried and covered with a woollen hat
The baby is dried fully, then wrapped in the bag including the head
The bag is used only after the baby reaches the unit
The bag replaces the radiant warmer
read.explanation: From the manual's box "Preparation for specific neonatal conditions" (preterm < 32 weeks or < 1500 g).

read.text: The infant born through meconium-stained amniotic fluid:

• Do not perform routine suctioning of the mouth, nose, or trachea.
  • Assess the newborn immediately and initiate standard resuscitation steps.
  • Focus on establishing effective ventilation as the priority intervention.
  • Suction the airway only when there is obvious obstruction or when ventilation is ineffective due to meconium.
  • Ensure intubation equipment is available if advanced airway intervention is required.
A baby is born through meconium-stained amniotic fluid. Should you suction the mouth, nose and trachea routinely?
options: No: assess, start the standard steps and focus on effective ventilation; suction only for obvious obstruction or ineffective ventilation
Yes: always suction the trachea before the first breath
Yes: suction the mouth and nose only
Only if the baby is vigorous
read.explanation: The manual: "Do not perform routine suctioning of the mouth, nose, or trachea."

read.text: Multiple births

• Provide a fully equipped resuscitator for each infant if possible
  • At least one person with advanced resuscitation skills must be available for each infant

read.label: Standard operating procedure
read.text: Bag and mask · from the manual, Module 2, Section 8: Equipment

• Fit the mask over the nose and mouth. Press firmly to prevent air leaks.
  • Hold with the thumb on one side and the index and middle fingers on the other.
  • With the other hand, squeeze the bag at a rate of 30 to 60 breaths/minute for 60 seconds. Ventilation is effective if the chest rises and falls.
IMPORTANT

• excessive ventilation pressure can cause a pneumothorax.
    • If the chest fails to rise:
        • Check the connection between the bag and the mask.
        • Correct the position of the mask on the face.
        • Correct the head position.
    • Check every minute for spontaneous respiratory effort (look for chest movement); do not take the mask off the neonate’s face to check for spontaneous breathing.
    • Continue manual ventilation until there is spontaneous respiratory effort.
Bag and Mask Disinfection

• Rinse the components under running (tap) water to remove gross soil.
  • soak the device in in soupy solution, for the removal of residues of dried blood with using a soft brush until all visible soil is removed.
  • Rinse the components with running (tap) water for one minute.
  • Fully immerse the device in disinfection solution for the 20 minutes
  • Rinse the device by fully immersing it in distill water and repeat for a total of 3 rinses using a fresh batch of distill water each time.
  • Dry the device using a sterile cloth.
  • Autoclave can be used with running a full cycle at 134 – 135 °C with an exposure time of 10 minutes and a dry time of 45 minutes.
Bag and mask ventilation: what rate, and how do you know it is effective?
options: 30–60 breaths a minute; the chest rises and falls
100 breaths a minute; the baby cries
10 breaths a minute; the bag empties
read.explanation: If the chest does not rise: check the bag–mask connection, the mask position and the head position. Excessive pressure can cause a pneumothorax.

read.text: Suction bulb · from the manual, Module 2, Section 8: Equipment

A reusable, hand-held, manual suction device designed to suck gently and clear excessive mucus from the airway of a newborn to facilitate easier breathing. The life span of the device is minimum 3 years or 20 autoclave sessions, whichever comes first. Standard procedure

• 1. Always use clean disinfected Bulb
  • 2. squeeze the air out of the bulb. Keep the bulb squeezed.
  • 3. Gently place the tip of the squeezed bulb into a nostril.

• 4. Let go of the bulb to let the air back into it. This will pull the mucus out of the nose and into the bulb.
    • 5. Squeeze the mucus out of the bulb and onto a tissue.
    • 6. Suction the other nostril the same way.
    • 7. If mucus is too thick to suction, you can thin it with saline
  • 8. Gently wipe off the mucus around the baby’s nose with tissues to prevent irritation.
Disinfection of The Suction Bulb

• Wash the bulb syringe in warm, soapy water after each use.
  • Squeeze soapy water into the bulb and shake to clean out the mucus. Then, squeeze the water out.
  • Put in chlorine solution foe 20 minutes
  • Rinse the bulb many times by filling it with clear water, then squeezing the water out.
  • Also, can be autoclaved at 136°C

sections.title: Early essential newborn care and the initial steps

read.text: Early Essential Newborn Care EENC is a package of evidence-based interventions aimed at improving the health and survival of newborns, particularly in the first few minutes and hours after birth. These interventions focus on preventing newborn deaths due to common issues like hypothermia, infection, and breathing problems.

• 1. Immediate care at birth
    • a. thorough drying
    • b. stimulation
  • 2. suction if needed
  • 3. delayed cord clamping (after 1-3 minutes)
  • 4. Thermal care through immediate uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact
  • 5. Support early breastfeeding within (within first hour)
  • 6. Resuscitation when needed
Keep the baby warm all the time
1.3.1 Initial Steps for Vigorous, Term Newborns
All 3 rapid evaluation questions must be “Yes”: Term? Tone good? Breathing/crying?
When vigorous, the newborn stays with the mother (skin-to-skin).

• 1. Provide Warmth
  • Maintain skin-to-skin contact on the mother’s chest/abdomen.
  • Cover with a warm towel/blanket.
  • 2. Dry and Stimulate
  • Dry thoroughly to reduce heat loss.
  • Gentle stimulation (rubbing back or extremities) to encourage effective breathing.
  • 3. Open the Airway
  • Position on mother’s chest with neutral head position
  • 4. Clear Secretions (if needed only)
  • Wipe mouth and nose with cloth.
  • Bulb suction only if secretions obstruct breathing or the newborn struggles to clear them.
  • 5. Ongoing Monitoring
  • Continue assessing breathing, tone, activity, color, and temperature.
  • Initiate additional interventions if status changes.
A vigorous term baby is on the mother's chest. When do you use bulb suction?
options: Only if secretions obstruct breathing or the baby struggles to clear them
Always, as soon as the baby is born
read.explanation: The manual: "Bulb suction only if secretions obstruct breathing or the newborn struggles to clear them." Wipe the mouth and nose with a cloth.

read.text: 1.3.2 Umbilical Cord Management: Delayed Cord Clamping (DCC)

sections.title: Delayed cord clamping: definition and evidence

read.text: Definition

Physiologically, early cord clamping (ECC) has been defined as clamping of the cord when there is still circulation of blood from the placenta to the newborn, and delayed cord clamping (DCC) has been defined as clamping of the cord after the stoppage of placental circulation.
Physiological background:
At the time of birth, a large volume of the baby's blood remains in the placenta.

If maternal blood is still flowing to the placenta and the umbilical cord has not been clamped, placenta! Gas exchange will continue, and additional oxygenated blood will be returned to the baby through the umbilical vein.
This blood may play an important role in the newborn baby's transition from fetal to neonatal circulation.
In term newborns, DCC for one-minute leads to the transfer of 80 ml of extra blood, and a delay of three minutes leads to the total transfer of 100 ml of blood to the neonate.
In a term newborn, how much extra blood reaches the baby when the cord is clamped after one minute, and after three minutes?
options: 80 ml after one minute; 100 ml in total after three minutes
None: blood flows back to the placenta
read.explanation: The manual: "DCC for one-minute leads to the transfer of 80 ml of extra blood, and a delay of three minutes leads to the total transfer of 100 ml."

read.text: Evidence:
The present studies that compared ECC and DCC have defined ECC as cord clamping immediately or within 15 seconds of birth and DCC as cord clamping after 30 seconds to 3 minutes after neonatal birth.
Cochrane meta-analysis included fifteen studies and showed that DCC was associated

• Fewer infants requiring transfusions for anaemia (RR 0.61)
  • The hemoglobin concentration in infants at 24 to 48 hours was significantly higher in the DCC group.
  • less intraventricular hemorrhages (IVH) (ultrasound diagnosis all grades) (RR 0.59)
  • lower risk for necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) (RR 0.62) compared with ECC.
  • There was a significant increase in mean birth weight in DCC (101 grams)
  • The peak bilirubin concentration was significantly higher in neonates allocated to DCC compared with ECC (mean difference 15.01 mmol/L)
The Cochrane meta-analysis that sought the effect of DCC in term neonates reported no significant differences in :

• neonatal mortality
  • Apgar score < 7 at five minutes
  • neonatal admission.
What did the Cochrane meta-analysis find for delayed cord clamping compared with early clamping?
read.answer: Fewer transfusions for anaemia (RR 0.61), higher haemoglobin at 24–48 hours, less IVH (RR 0.59), lower NEC (RR 0.62) and a higher mean birth weight (101 g); but a higher peak bilirubin. In term neonates there was no significant difference in neonatal mortality, Apgar < 7 at five minutes, or neonatal admission.

sections.title: Delayed cord clamping: recommendations and contraindications

read.text: NRP recommendations regarding delayed cord clamping (DCC):
The 2023 NRP recommendations for delayed cord clamping decision have depended on several factors:

• 1. The most beneficial action for the newborn
  • 2. The gestational age (term or near term, preterm, less than 34 weeks, or between 28 to 34 weeks of gestation)
  • 3. Whether Resuscitation is required or not
  • 4. The need for positive pressure ventilation.
The NRP recommendations regarding delayed umbilical cord clamping DCC are:

• For term and late preterm newborn infants ≥34 weeks’ gestation who do not require resuscitation
  • delayed cord clamping (≥30 seconds) can be beneficial compared with early cord clamping (<30 seconds).
  • Intact cord milking is not known to be beneficial compared with delayed cord clamping (≥30 seconds).
  • For non-vigorous term and late preterm newborn infants (35–42 weeks’ gestation),
    • intact cord milking may be reasonable compared with early cord clamping (<30 seconds).
  • For preterm newborn infants <34 weeks’ gestation who do not require resuscitation
    • delaying cord clamping (≥30 seconds) can be beneficial compared with early cord clamping (<30 seconds).
  • For preterm newborn infants between 28 and 34 weeks’ gestation who do not require resuscitation and in whom delayed cord clamping cannot be performed
    • intact cord milking may be reasonable.
  • For preterm newborn infants <28 weeks’ gestation
    • intact cord milking is not recommended.
  • Effective positive-pressure ventilation is the priority in newborn infants who need support after birth.

options: No: for preterm infants < 28 weeks intact cord milking is not recommended
Yes, instead of delayed cord clamping
Only if the mother is bleeding
read.explanation: NRP recommendations in the manual. For < 34 weeks without resuscitation, delaying cord clamping (≥ 30 seconds) can be beneficial.

read.text: Contraindications to Delayed Cord Clamping (DCC)
Delayed cord clamping is the standard of care for most newborns. Immediate cord clamping should be performed only in the presence of the following absolute contraindications:

• Severe maternal hemorrhage requiring immediate life-saving intervention
  • Placental abruption with active bleeding
  • Uterine rupture
  • Maternal cardiac arrest or profound hemodynamic instability
  • Newborn requiring immediate resuscitation that cannot be provided with the cord intact
  • Apnea or gasping respirations with heart rate <100 beats per minute
  • Umbilical cord avulsion or complete placental separation preventing placental transfusion

IMPORTANT Remember:
Resuscitation with the umbilical cord intact should be considered whenever feasible Maternal safety always takes precedence over neonatal benefit

sections.title: Thermoregulation: normal temperature and why hypothermia matters

read.text: Introduction
Thermoregulation is the ability to maintain a balance between heat production and heat loss.
The maintenance of body temperature within a normal range will minimize both metabolic and oxygen consumption (neutral thermal zone).
Current recommendations are to maintain core temperature between 36.5 and 37.5 °C at all times except in the context of therapeutic hypothermia.
Definition of hypothermia
Hypothermia is defined as a temperature < 36.5 °C.
What core temperature should a newborn be kept at, and below what temperature is it hypothermia?
read.explanation: The manual: maintain core temperature between 36.5 and 37.5 °C; hypothermia is a temperature < 36.5 °C.

read.text: Measuring temperature

Whilst an axillary digital thermometer temperature approximates rectal temperature in otherwise healthy infants, for very preterm infants on admission, it has been reported that axillary temperature has a sensitivity of 65% when used to detect rectal hyperthermia and 100% sensitivity for hypothermia
Importance

• Extremely preterm infants who are hypothermic on admission have an increased risk of death and neurodevelopmental impairment
  • Hypothermia leads to a significant increase in Apgar score less than 7, IVH, late onset sepsis, hypoglycemia, and respiratory distress ( see figure ..)
  • Very preterm infants, as well as infants born in low-resource settings who are hyperthermic on admission, are also at increased risk of mortality.
  • Admission temperature in the NICU is a strong predictor of neonatal mortality. The highest risk of neonatal hypothermia is within the first minutes to hours after birth, as there is a wide difference between in-utero and environmental temperature
  • Thermal care interventions in the delivery room for preterm neonates are associated with improved core body temperature.

sections.title: Hypothermia: risk factors and the four ways a baby loses heat

read.text: Risk Factors for Hypothermia

• Newborn infants, especially those born premature, low birth weight, and/or sick. The reported incidence of hypothermia at the time of admission to the NICU in VLBW newborns ranges from 31% to 78%
  • Infants exposed to maternal chorioamnionitis,
  • Advanced neonatal resuscitation,
    • Delivery room temperature < 25 degree C, There is a 28% increase in neonatal mortality with each 1 °C fall in axillary temperature while admitted in NICU
    • Cold or un-humidified gases in the delivery room and during transport.
The following characteristics put newborns at a greater risk of heat loss:

• A large surface area-to-body mass ratio
  • Decreased subcutaneous fat
  • Greater body water content
  • Immature skin leading to increased evaporative water and heat losses
  • Poorly developed metabolic mechanism for responding to thermal stress (e.g., no shivering)
  • Altered skin blood-flow (e.g., peripheral cyanosis)
Classification of abnormal temperature and Hypothermia
Sources of heat loss
There are four ways in which a newborn loses body heat:

• 1 Conduction: when the newborn is placed naked on a cooler surface, such as a table, a scale, a cold bed. The transfer of heat between two solid objects that are touching is influenced by the size of the surface area in contact and the temperature gradient between surfaces.
  • 2 Convection: when the newborn is exposed to cool surrounding air or to a draft from open doors, windows, or fans, the transfer of heat from the newborn to air or liquid is affected by the newborn’s large surface area, air flow (drafts, ventilation system, etc), and temperature gradient.
  • 3 Evaporation: when amniotic fluid evaporates from the skin. Evaporative losses may be insensible (from skin and breathing) or sensible (sweating). Other factors that contribute to evaporative loss are the newborn’s surface area, vapor pressure, and air velocity. This is the greatest source of heat loss at birth.
  • 4 Radiation: when the newborn is near cool objects, walls, tables, and cabinets, without actually being in contact with them. The transfer of heat between solid surfaces that are not touching. Factors that affect heat change due to radiation are the temperature gradient between the two surfaces, the surface area of the solid surfaces, and the distance between the solid surfaces. This is the greatest source of heat loss after birth.
How is the baby losing heat? Sort each situation.

read.text: Prevention and management of hypothermia

• 1. Thermal care interventions in the delivery room for preterm neonates are associated with improved core body temperature. Specifically, use of a plastic bag or wrap with a plastic cap or with heated, humidified gas was associated with a lower risk of major brain injury and mortality.
  • 2. Care should be taken when using multiple interventions to avoid hyperthermia
  • 3. The “warm chain” (WHO, 1997). And the updated NRP guidelines for the prevention and management of hypothermia are used as the main reference in this module.
  • 4. The warm chain is a set of interlinked procedures to be performed at birth and during the next few hours and days after birth in order to minimize heat loss in all newborns
Delivery room prevention and management of hypothermia

For otherwise healthy infants, including vigorous late preterm infants, early skin-to-skin contact after delivery increased infant temperature +0.3OC and promoted breastfeeding without complications. Routine monitoring of otherwise healthy infants to detect hypothermia can be done with an axillary digital thermometer.
The following interventions are targeted at minimizing heat loss, optimizing heat gain, and preventing hypothermia (also called the ‘warm chain’): see table below

• 1. The birth environment should be ≥ 25-degree C.
  • 2. For infants born < 32 weeks and /or <1500 g – place in plastic wrap/polyethylene bag (Neohelp™)
  • 3. Immediately drying for infants and put into skin-to-skin contact if not immediately placed in a plastic wrap/polyethylene bag.

• 4. In lower and middle-income countries, NRP 2015 recommends the use of clean food-grade plastic bags up to the level of the neck and skin-to-skin contact to prevent hypothermia
  • 5. Uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact for at least 60 minutes.
  • 6. Breastfeeding within the first hour, where appropriate
  • 7. If on radiant heater resuscitator, ensure radiant heater on and correct heating setting (note that different systems have different heat outputs so familiarize yourself to the system). Rephrasing (If using a radiant warmer during resuscitation, ensure it is switched on and set to the appropriate heat level. Be aware that different devices have varying heat outputs, so always familiarize yourself with the specific system in use. )
  • 8. If placed in a transport incubator, a pre-warm incubator.
  • 9. Ensure all linen and resuscitation equipment, including surfactant pre-warmed, and use warm, humidified gases when possible

sections.title: Skin-to-skin contact and the warm chain

read.text: Uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact for 60-90 minutes

The World Health Organization (WHO) strongly recommends uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact (SSC) for all mothers and newborns immediately after birth. The WHO advises that this initial contact should be prolonged and uninterrupted for at least 90 minutes, or ideally longer.

Immediate “skin-to-skin” after delivery is when a newborn is dried and placed naked on the mother’s bare abdomen, and the two are covered with a blanket for warmth. Skin-to-skin care is critical for achieving newborn homeostasis and thermoregulation in the first hours of life.
It is the best practice available to facilitate a smooth transition to life outside of the uterus and get breastfeeding off to a great start.
Benefits of Skin-to-skin Care

• 1. Thermoregulation: Higher axillary temperatures – lowered risk for hypothermia Higher blood glucose levels – lowered risk for hypoglycemia
  • 2. Cardio-respiratory stability: Lower, more stable respiratory rates
  • 3. Faster return to physiologically normal heart rate
  • 4. Decreased crying
  • 5. Facilitates self-attachment for breastfeeding, the warmth, smell, and closeness to the breast are associated with easier and longer breastfeeding
  • 6. Lower cortisol levels in both mother and infant
  • 7. Decreased anxiety for birthing parent
  • 8. Initiates the development of a healthy newborn microbiome
  • 9. Increased self-confidence in the mother’s parenting ability
  • 10. Stimulation of maternal oxytocin to enhance uterine contractions, access to colostrum, and mother-baby bonding – allows mother and baby to smell and feel each other
For how long does WHO advise uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact after birth?
read.explanation: The manual: WHO advises the initial contact should be prolonged and uninterrupted for at least 90 minutes, or ideally longer.

read.text: Ten Steps of the Warm Chain (WHO)

1. Warm delivery room• Temperature ≥ 25°C, free from drafts from open windows, doors, or fans.
• Prepare supplies in advance to keep the newborn warm.
Adults should not determine temperature based on their comfort.
2. Immediate dryingImmediately dry the newborn after birth with a warm towel/cloth to prevent evaporation heat loss (for <29 wks. GA refers to NRP guidelines).
3. Skin-to-skin contact• Place the newborn on the mother's chest/abdomen while drying to prevent heat loss (if the mother is unable, the partner may do so).
• Cover with a second towel and put a cap on the head to prevent convective heat loss. Keep newborn skin-to-skin with mother and covered.
• Minimize uncovering during assessments/interventions.
• Maintain skin-to-skin during:
• Placenta delivery/suturing
• Transfer to the postnatal unit/recovery room
• Assessments/interventions First hours after birth
4. BreastfeedingInitiate as soon as possible, preferably within 1 hour of birth.
5. Postpone weighing and bathing• Weigh after uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact and first feed; use a warm blanket on a scale.
• Bathing soon after birth causes a temperature drop → risk of hypothermia/hypoglycemia.
• Delay bathing until 6–8 hrs or when stable.
• If hypothermic with thick wet hair → wash/dry hair only, then cover the head. Bathe quickly in a warm room with warm water (tub bathing preferred for stable newborns; water should cover shoulders).
• After bath → dry thoroughly, place skin-to-skin (or double wrap with warm blankets and cover head).
After skin-to-skin → dress, cap, and wrap the newborn in a dry ,warm blanket.
6. Appropriate clothing/blanketDress in loose clothing and a blanket.
7. Mother and newborn together• Keep together 24 hrs/day (rooming-in) in a warm room (≥ 25°C).
• Feed on demand.
Skin-to-skin can rewarm mild–moderate hypothermia (see table 3).
Warm transportation• Keep warm while waiting for transport.
Dress and wrap in blankets if a transport device is used.
Warm assessment (if not skin-to-skin)• Place the newborn on a warm surface in a warm room.
• Add extra heat source if needed (radiant warmer).
Use servo-control if the radiant warmer is >10 minutes.
In the warm chain, when should the first bath be given?
options: Delay bathing until 6–8 hours or when stable
read.explanation: Step 5, "Postpone weighing and bathing": bathing soon after birth causes a temperature drop, with a risk of hypothermia and hypoglycaemia.

sections.title: Shock: definition, causes and signs

read.text: Definition:

• Shock, or circulatory failure, is defined as a physiologic state characterized by tissue hypoxia due to reduced oxygen delivery and/or increased oxygen consumption or inadequate oxygen utilization.
  • Shock is often initially reversible, but must be recognized and treated immediately to prevent progression to irreversible organ dysfunction.
  • Hypotension is a late sign
  • It's a major cause of neonatal death, with early recognition crucial for survival, involving fluid resuscitation, cardiovascular support(vasopressors), and addressing underlying infection.
A baby has cold extremities, a capillary refill of 4 seconds and a fast heart rate, but a normal blood pressure. Can this be shock?
options: Yes: hypotension is a late sign, so shock must be recognised before the blood pressure falls
No: shock needs a low blood pressure
Only if the baby is preterm
read.explanation: The manual: "Hypotension is a late sign." Shock is often reversible at first, but must be recognised and treated immediately.

read.text: Causes & Risk Factors

• Maternal Factors: GBS infection, chorioamnionitis, prolonged rupture of membranes.
  • Infant Factors: Prematurity, low birth weight, male gender, indwelling lines (catheters, tubes).
  • Pathogens: Bacteria from the mother's genital tract (early-onset), hospital-acquired (late-onset).
Signs & Symptoms (Can be subtle)

• General: Fever or low temperature, lethargy, irritability, poor feeding, vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice, pale/clammy skin, swelling.
  • Respiratory: Fast/slow breathing, apnea, grunting, nasal flaring.
  • Cardiovascular (Shock): Fast/slow heart rate, cold extremities, poor capillary refill, mottling, hypotension, warm extremities (early warm shock).
  • Metabolic: Hypo/hyperglycemia, acidosis, electrolyte imbalance.
Management Priorities (Emergency Care)

• 1. Antibiotics: Immediate, broad-spectrum antibiotics.
  • 2. Fluid Resuscitation: Volume expanders to improve circulation.
  • 3. Cardiovascular Support: Vasopressors (like dopamine, epinephrine) for persistent hypotension, possibly inhaled nitric oxide for high pulmonary pressures (PPHN).
  • 4. Ventilation: Support for respiratory distress.
  • 5. Monitoring: Close hemodynamic monitoring metabolic support, (echocardiography), & managing complications like PPHN.
Treatment Details:
Stabilization: Airway + O2 if hypoxemic, mechanical ventilation/respiratory support if needed.
Circulation: IV access, initial lab samples, central line (if possible: for frequent blood samples and Arterial line: for central BP measurement).
Ongoing evaluation: continues evaluation is necessary, management may change frequently.

      • Administration of hypertonic solutions (e.g. glucose >12.5%, parenteral nutrition or inotropes)
  • Contraindications:
      • Omphalitis
      • Peritonitis
      • possible/confirmed necrotizing enterocolitis
      • intestinal hypoperfusion
      • Umbilical sepsis
  • Complications:
      • Infection
      • Bleeding
      • perforation of vessel
      • thrombosis with distal embolization
      • ischemia or infarction of lower extremities, bowel, or kidney
      • arrhythmia if catheter is in the heart; air embolism.
  • Equipment and supplies
      • High-level disinfected or sterile umbilical catheter or ordinary gastric tube:
          • If the baby weighs less than 1.5 kg, use a 3.5-F catheter
          • If the baby weighs 1.5 kg or more, use a 5-F catheter
      • Sterile infusion set with IV fluid (use a micro dropper if one is available)
      • Sterile 5- or 10-ml syringe
      • Sterile drapes
      • Sterile blade
      • Cord tie or suture (to control bleeding)
      • Sterile forceps
      • Sterile suture, adhesive strapping, or thin paper tape (to secure catheter)
  • Preparation :
      • Determine Umbilical venous catheter (UVC) site: lines should be placed in the inferior vena cava above the level of the ductus venosus and the hepatic veins and below the level of the right atrium.
      • Determine Catheter length:
          • Determine the length of catheter required using either a standardized graph based on shoulder-umbilical length or
          • use distance between xiphisternum and umbilicus +1, plus stump, or
          • The following birth weight (BW) regression formula:
          • 1. UAC high line (cm) = (3 x BW [kg]) + 9
          • 2. UVC length (cm) = 0.5 x UAC high line (cm) + 1
PRACTISE THIS SKILL Procedure for UVC line

• Determine the length of the catheter to be inserted
  • Restrain infants. Maintain the infant’s temperature during the procedure. Prepare and drape the umbilical cord and adjacent skin using sterile technique.
  • Flush the catheter with sterile saline solution before insertion. Ensure that there are no air bubbles in the catheter or attached syringe.
  • Tie sterile umbilical tape around the base of the cord, tight enough to prevent bleeding. Cut through the cord horizontally about 1.5 to 2 cm from the skin.
  • Isolate the thin-walled UV, clear thrombi with forceps, and insert catheter, aiming the tip toward the right shoulder. Gently advance the catheter to the desired distance. Do not force. If resistance is encountered, try loosening the umbilical tape, applying steady and gentle pressure, or manipulating the angle of the umbilical cord to the skin. Resistance is commonly met at the abdominal wall and again at the portal system. Do not infuse anything into the liver.
  • As the catheter is advanced, periodically apply gentle suction with the syringe until blood flows back. Once blood flows back freely through the catheter (usually after the catheter is inserted 5 to 7 cm), do not advance the catheter any further.
  • If resistance is encountered while advancing the catheter, especially in the first 2 to 3 cm, do not continue. Remove the catheter and try again.
  • Tie the cord tie or suture around the stump of the umbilicus to hold the catheter in place and prevent bleeding around the catheter or from one of the arteries.
  • Remove the syringe and connect the infusion set to the catheter, ensuring that there are no air bubbles in the set.
  • Secure the catheter with suture material or adhesive tape to prevent it from being dislodged.
  • Confirm catheter tip position with x-ray or ultrasound.
  • The catheter may be pulled back but not advanced once the sterile field is broken.
  • Look for redness and swelling around the umbilicus, which may indicate infection. If redness or swelling is seen at any time, stop the infusion and remove the umbilical vein catheter. Attempt to establish a peripheral IV line again, and treat for infection of the umbilicus

read.question: For the same 2 kg baby (UAC high line 15 cm), how long is the UVC?
read.explanation: UVC length (cm) = 0.5 × UAC high line + 1 = 0.5 × 15 + 1 = 8.5 cm.

read.explanation: The other three are indications in the manual. Contraindications: omphalitis, peritonitis, possible or confirmed NEC, intestinal hypoperfusion, umbilical sepsis.

read.label: Standard operating procedure
read.text: Intraosseous access · from the manual, Module 2, Section 7: Neonatal Procedures

Indications: Establishing intravenous access in a newborn baby can be difficult. In an emergency, a good temporary alternative is the intraosseous route using the bone marrow cavity. Fluid and drugs can be given by this route. Remove the intraosseous line as soon as other IV access is established (within eight hours, if possible).
Contraindication: Do not place an intraosseous line if there is infection at the intended insertion site or if the bone is fractured
Complications:

• Extravasation of fluid from incomplete or through-and-through cortex penetration
  • Infection
  • Bleeding
  • Osteomyelitis
  • compartment syndrome
  • fat embolism
  • Fracture
  • epiphyseal injury
Preparation: Determine Sites of entry (in order of preference):

• Anteromedial surface of the proximal tibia, 1 to 2 cm below and slightly medial to the tibial tuberosity on the flat part of the bone
      • Distal femur 3 cm above the lateral condyle in the midline
      • Medial surface of the distal tibia 1 to 2 cm above the medial malleolus (may be a more effective site in older children than the distal femur)
      • Proximal humerus, 2 cm below the acromion process into the greater tubercle with the arm held in adduction and internal rotation
      • Anterior Superior iliac spine at a 90-degree angle to the long axis of the Body
  • Prepare the solution to be infused, ensuring that the entire infusion set is filled with fluid and that there is no air in the infusion set.
  • Prepare the skin over the insertion site using a swab or cotton-wool ball soaked in antiseptic solution, and allow it to dry.
PRACTISE THIS SKILL Procedure:

• Prepare the selected site in a sterile fashion.
  • If the child is conscious, anesthetize the puncture site down to the periosteum with 1% lidocaine (optional in emergent situations).
  • Position the baby’s leg with the knee bent about 30 degrees and the heel resting on the table. Support the upper tibia with one hand, placed so that the hand is not directly behind the site insertion.
  • Insert an 18-gauge (for infants and neonates) IO needle perpendicular to the skin at an angle away from the epiphyseal plate, and advance to the periosteum. With a boring rotary motion, penetrate through the cortex until there is a decrease in resistance, indicating that you have reached the marrow. The needle should stand firmly without support. Secure the needle carefully.
  • attempt to aspirate marrow. (Note that it is not necessary to aspirate marrow.) Flush with crystalloid solution. Observe fluid extravasation. Marrow can be sent to determine glucose levels, chemistries, blood types and crossmatches, hemoglobin levels, blood gas analyses, and cultures.
  • slowly inject 3 ml of IV fluid to check for proper placement of needle
  • Look for swelling (indicating leaking of fluid under the skin) at the front of the leg or in the calf muscle at the back of the leg. If swelling is seen, remove the needle and try again;
  • If it is difficult to infuse the fluid but there is no swelling in the calf muscle, the needle may have entered the posterior bone cortex. Withdraw the needle approximately 0.5 cm and cautiously inject IV fluid again.
  • If no problems are detected, Secure the IO needle. Attach standard IV tubing.
Increased pressure (through pressure bag or push) may be necessary for infusion.
There is a high risk for obstruction if continuous high-pressure fluids are not flushed through the IO needle.
• Remove the intraosseous needle as soon as alternative IV access is available, and within eight hours, if possible.
Where is the first-choice site for intraosseous access in a newborn?
options: The anteromedial proximal tibia, 1–2 cm below and slightly medial to the tibial tuberosity
read.explanation: Remove the IO line as soon as other IV access is established, within eight hours if possible.

sections.title: Hypoglycaemia: definition and severity

read.text: INTRODUCTION

Neonatal hypoglycemia is one of the most common metabolic emergencies in the newborn period. If not promptly recognized and treated, it can lead to irreversible neurological injury, seizures, developmental delay, and death. In Sudan, where resource limitations may affect screening and monitoring, a high index of suspicion and a systematic approach are essential.

This section provides a standardized, evidence-based, and context-adapted protocol for the identification, investigation, and management of neonatal hypoglycemia in Sudanese NICUs and newborn care units.
DEFINITION
Hypoglycemia is defined as a plasma glucose level below the following thresholds:

PopulationThreshold (mmol/L)Threshold (mg/dL)
Term newborn (≥37 weeks)< 2 mmol/L< 36 mg/dL
Preterm newborn (<37 weeks)< 2.6 mmol/L< 46.8 mg/dL
Below what blood glucose is a preterm newborn hypoglycaemic, and a term newborn?
read.explanation: From the manual's definition table. Severe hypoglycaemia is < 1 mmol/L (< 18 mg/dL).

read.text: Severity classification:

• Moderate hypoglycemia: 1 – 2.6 mmol/L (18 – 46 mg/dL)
  • Severe hypoglycemia: < 1 mmol/L (< 18 mg/dL)
IMPORTANT In the first 48 hours of life, transitional low glucose levels are common. However, treatment thresholds should be followed to prevent harm.
RISK FACTORS (SCREENING INDICATIONS)
Screen for hypoglycemia in all newborns with risk factors, even if asymptomatic:

sections.title: Hypoglycaemia: who to screen, and the signs

read.text: High-Risk Categories:

• Prematurity (<37 weeks) or low birth weight (<2500 g)
  • Infant of a diabetic mother (gestational or pre-existing diabetes)
  • Large for gestational age (LGA) or macrosomia (birth weight >4 kg)
  • Small for gestational age (SGA) / intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR)
  • Perinatal asphyxia (Apgar score ≤5 at 5 min, needed resuscitation)
  • Hypothermia (temperature <36.5°C)
  • Respiratory distress (requiring oxygen or respiratory support)
  • Suspected sepsis
  • Poor feeding or delayed initiation of breastfeeding
  • Family history of hypoglycemia or metabolic disorders
  • Congenital syndromes (e.g., Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome)
  • Polycythemia (hematocrit >65%)
  • Erythroblastosis fetalis
Sudan-specific consideration: In settings with high rates of maternal malnutrition, low birth weight, and limited antenatal care, a lower threshold for screening is recommended.
Should this baby be screened for hypoglycaemia (even with no signs)?
groups: No risk factor in this list

items.text: Born at 35 weeks
Mother has gestational diabetes
Birth weight 4.3 kg
Temperature 36.1 °C
Term, 3.2 kg, breastfeeding well, mother well

read.explanation: All the first four are high-risk categories in the manual. In Sudan, a lower threshold for screening is recommended.

read.text: CLINICAL PRESENTATION
Symptoms may be nonspecific. Assume hypoglycemia in any neonate with altered behavior.
Neurogenic (Autonomic) Symptoms:

• Jitteriness, tremors
  • Irritability, high-pitched cry
  • Sweating
  • Tachycardia, tachypnea
  • Pallor
Neuroglycopenic Symptoms (Brain dysfunction):

• Lethargy, hypotonia
  • Poor feeding, weak suck
  • Apnea, bradycardia
  • Hypothermia
  • Seizures
  • Coma
IMPORTANT In preterm infants, symptoms may be subtle or absent. Routine screening is essential.
Which of these is a neuroglycopenic sign (brain dysfunction) rather than a neurogenic (autonomic) one?
read.explanation: Neuroglycopenic: lethargy, hypotonia, poor feeding, apnoea, bradycardia, hypothermia, seizures, coma. Assume hypoglycaemia in any neonate with altered behaviour.

sections.title: Hypoglycaemia: measuring glucose and managing the baby without signs

read.text: DIAGNOSIS AND MONITORING
Glucose Measurement

• Preferred sample: Plasma glucose (laboratory) – most accurate.
  • Point-of-care (glucometer): Use for screening, but confirm low values with laboratory glucose if available.
  • Heel-prick capillary sample: Ensure warm heel, wipe away first drop, collect second drop.
Timing of screening:

• First screen: At 1–2 hours of age (or before first feed if symptomatic).
  • Repeat before feeds every 3–6 hours in at-risk infants until stable for 12–24 hours.
  • In symptomatic infants, check glucose immediately
When to Suspect Persistent Hypoglycemia Disorder

• Hypoglycemia recurring beyond 48 hours of life.
  • Requiring intravenous dextrose infusion >8 mg/kg/min.
  • No obvious risk factors.
  • Family history of hypoglycemia or consanguinity.
  • Dysmorphic features (e.g., macroglossia, midline defects).
If suspected, collect critical sample during hypoglycemia.
MANAGEMENT algorithm of Asymptomatic Hypoglycaemia

• Dry baby and keep warm immediately after birth and Skin-to-skin contact for at least 1 hour.
  • Ensure baby offered feed within first hour after birth, then offer breast in response to feeding cues as often as possible
    • If mother has breast feeding difficulties because of her condition, her breasts or the baby, nurses should teach her on proper attachment and positioning and the other problems.
    • If breast feeding has failed mother should be encouraged to express milk and give by cup, spoon or syringe and ensure 2-3 hrly feeds.
    • If there is contraindication to breast milk, or it is insufficient, give 40–60 mL/kg/day 3-hrly over first 24 hr after birth, increasing to 70–90 mL/kg/day in 24–48 hr after birth, and 100–120 mL/kg/day in first 48–72 hr after birth.Baby may require NGT feeding to maintain adequate blood glucose levels
  • Blood glucose monitoring
    • check first blood glucose 30 minutes after completion of first feed, which should be initiated within first hour after birth.
    • If feeding is delayed beyond the first hour, check the blood glucose at one hour, then 30 minutes after first feed.
    • Check blood glucose level before 3rd feed.
  • If ≥2.0 mmol/L (in ≥37 weeks), or ≥2.6 mmol/L(in <37 weeks) : Continue to support responsive breastfeeding
  • Observe for clinical signs of hypoglycaemia and continue monitoring blood glucose as required.
  • Do not allow >3 hr between feeds until 2 consecutive blood glucose measurements ≥2.0 mmol/L (in ≥37 weeks) or ≥2.6 mmol/L(in <37 weeks), and at least 24-48 hr of successful feeding to be demonstrated before discharge
  • If baby shows clinical signs suggestive of hypoglycaemia, measure blood glucose immediately and Administer 40% oral glucose gel
    • 0.5 ml/kg of 40% glucose gel
    • Max 2 doses per episode, 6 doses in 48 hours
    • Administer via oral syringe, massage into cheek, follow with feed
    • Recheck glucose 30 minutes post-feed
When is the first blood glucose checked in an at-risk baby without signs who fed in the first hour?
options: 30 minutes after the end of the first feed
read.explanation: The manual's algorithm: "check first blood glucose 30 minutes after completion of first feed". If feeding is delayed beyond the first hour, check at one hour, then 30 minutes after the first feed.

read.question: A 3 kg baby with signs of hypoglycaemia. What volume of 40% glucose gel is given (0.5 ml/kg)?
read.explanation: 0.5 ml/kg × 3 kg = 1.5 ml, by oral syringe massaged into the cheek, then a feed. Maximum 2 doses per episode and 6 in 48 hours; recheck 30 minutes after the feed.

read.title: Taking a Heel Blood Sample - Newborn Care Series

sections.title: Hypoglycaemia: severe or with signs

read.text: Symptomatic or Severe Hypoglycaemia (BG <1.0mmol/l or there are abnormal clinical signs)
If blood glucose <1.0 mmol/L at any gestation and/or clinical signs consistent with hypoglycaemia, treat as a CLINICAL EMERGENCY.

• Admit to NICU
  • obtain IV access
  • collect blood sample for Lab confirmation of blood glucose + Hypoglycaemia screening tests and Review needs to screen for/treat sepsis
  • Give bolus 2.5 ml/kg of 10% dextrose.
  • Follow with continuous infusion (10% dextrose at 60 mL/kg/day).
  • increase GIR by 2mg/kg/min (by increasing volume and/or concentration of glucose infusion) and recheck blood glucose after 30 min
  • Repeat cycle if blood glucose still <1 mmol/L or their abnormal clinical signs

read.question: A 2 kg baby has a blood glucose of 0.8 mmol/L. What volume of 10% dextrose is the bolus (2.5 ml/kg)?
read.explanation: 2.5 ml/kg × 2 kg = 5 ml of 10% dextrose, then a continuous infusion of 10% dextrose at 60 ml/kg/day, and recheck after 30 minutes.

read.text: If BG 1.0-2.5 mmol/l and no abnormal clinical signs:

• Increase glucose delivery (GIR) by 2mg/kg/min
  • continue oral feeds and recheck blood glucose after 30 min.
  • IV 10% dextrose bolus is not indicated here.
Blood glucose is 1.8 mmol/L and the baby has no abnormal signs. What does the manual say?
options: Increase the GIR by 2 mg/kg/min, continue oral feeds, recheck after 30 minutes; no IV bolus
Do nothing until the next feed
read.explanation: If BG 1.0–2.5 mmol/L and no abnormal clinical signs: increase GIR by 2 mg/kg/min; IV 10% dextrose bolus is not indicated.

read.text: If BG >2.5 mmol/l:

• Continue enteral feeds and slow wean IV infusion.
  • Continue to monitor blood glucose until infant is on full enteral feeds and blood glucose values are >2.5mmol/l , or 3.0mmol/l in cases of hyperinsulinism over several fast feed cycles for at least 24 hours.
If IV access unavailable and unable to feed orally/NG:

• Give buccal dextrose gel 40% (0.5 mL/kg = 200 mg/kg) if available, then feed.
  • If no gel available: Give 2 mL/kg of 10% dextrose orally/NG as a temporary measure.

read.label: Standard operating procedure
read.text: Syringe pump · from the manual, Module 2, Section 8: Equipment
Main part
PRACTISE THIS SKILL Procedure

• Pump can be used either on any horizontal surface or on the IV pole with pole clamp.
  • Plug power cord into a wall outlet
  • Turn the power switch on. Follow according to manual of the model.
  • Press “Number Set Key” (up and down arrows) to set desired flow rate.
  • Load syringe with medication or desired fluid.
  • Lift up the Syringe Securing Bar and rotate right 90o .
  • Place the syringe into the bed. Be
  • sure to insert the nozzle into the syringe slot.
  • Then press the release button on the plunger driver block and slide the driver blocks into position so that the end of the syringe plunger can be placed into the slot in the driver block.
  • Turn the Syringe Securing Bar to the left 90 degrees to secure the syringe barrel.
  • Make sure the syringe barrel is secure.
  • Press and hold the PURGE button to purge air from the syringe and associated tubing before connecting to patient.
  • Press “RUN” to start infusion.
  • After use clean and store in cardboard box if not required for babies.
Before connecting a syringe pump to the baby, what must you do?
options: Press and hold PURGE to remove air from the syringe and tubing
read.explanation: From the syringe pump procedure.

read.text: Cleaning the Syringe pump

• 1. Damp cloth soaked in soap-water used for cleansing panel
  • 2. Use disposal syringe and tubing

sections.title: Hypoglycaemia: no glucometer, weaning, and persistent low glucose

read.text: WHEN BLOOD GLUCOSE MONITORING IS UNAVAILABLE In resource-limited settings without glucometers/labs:

• Asymptomatic high-risk infant: Assume moderate hypoglycemia and start early frequent breastfeeding ± NG feeds. Monitor clinically.
  • Symptomatic infant (jittery, lethargic, seizures): Assume severe hypoglycemia. Give 2 mL/kg 10% dextrose IV/NG/orally and start IV fluids if possible. Treat as severe hypoglycemia.
MAINTENANCE AND WEANING OF IV DEXTROSE

• Target glucose range: 2.5–5.0 mmol/L (45–90 mg/dL).
  • Monitor glucose every 1–2 hours until stable, then every 3–6 hours.
  • Weaning:
    • When glucose stable >3.0 mmol/L for 12 hours, start to reduce IV rate by 10–20% every 6 hours while increasing enteral feeds.
    • Ensure infant tolerates full enteral feeds before stopping IV.
  • Discharge criteria:
  • Glucose >2.5 mmol/L for 24 hours on enteral feeds alone.
  • Feeding well, weight gaining.
Persistently Low Blood Glucose Measurement
• Defined as >2 measurements <2.0 mmol/L ≥37 weeks’ gestation or <2.6 mmol/L <37 weeks’ gestation within the first 48 hr of life
CRITICAL SAMPLE FOR PERSISTENT HYPOGLYCEMIA
Collect during hypoglycemia (glucose <2.5 mmol/L) before treatment:

• Plasma glucose (confirmatory)
  • Insulin
  • C-peptide
  • Beta-hydroxybutyrate
  • Free fatty acids
  • Cortisol
  • Growth hormone
  • Lactate
  • Ammonia
  • Urine ketones
Interpretation:

• High insulin + low ketones/FFA = Hyperinsulinism
  • Low cortisol/GH = Pituitary/adrenal insufficiency
  • High lactate = Gluconeogenesis disorder
  • High ketones + low FFA = Fatty acid oxidation disorder
An asymptomatic high-risk baby, in a unit with no glucometer. What do you do?
options: Assume moderate hypoglycaemia: early frequent breastfeeding ± NG feeds, and monitor clinically
Give a dextrose bolus to every high-risk baby
Refer for a glucose test before feeding
read.explanation: The manual: when blood glucose monitoring is unavailable. A symptomatic baby is treated as severe hypoglycaemia (2 ml/kg 10% dextrose IV/NG/orally).

read.text: When can the IV dextrose be weaned?
options: When glucose is stable > 3.0 mmol/L for 12 hours: reduce the IV rate by 10–20% every 6 hours while increasing feeds
As soon as glucose is above 1 mmol/L
read.explanation: From "Maintenance and weaning of IV dextrose".

sections.title: Hypoglycaemia: refractory cases, prevention and Sudan considerations

read.text: REFRACTORY HYPOGLYCEMIA
If glucose remains low despite >12 mg/kg/min of dextrose:

• Rule out hyperinsulinism:
    • Check critical sample (see below).
    • Consider glucagon 0.02 mg/kg IM/IV (may give diagnostic and therapeutic benefit).
  • Consider hydrocortisone 2.5 mg/kg IV twice daily if adrenal insufficiency suspected.
  • Consult pediatric endocrinology if available (telemedicine if needed).
  • If hyperinsulinism confirmed: Diazoxide (starting 5 mg/kg/day in divided doses) may be used under specialist guidance (monitor for fluid retention, pulmonary hypertension).
Glucose stays low despite more than 12 mg/kg/min of dextrose. What is this called, and what is ruled out first?
options: Refractory hypoglycaemia; rule out hyperinsulinism with the critical sample
read.explanation: From "Refractory hypoglycemia". Glucagon 0.02 mg/kg may be considered, and hydrocortisone if adrenal insufficiency is suspected.

read.text: PREVENTION

• Early breastfeeding within 1 hour of birth.
  • Kangaroo Mother Care for preterm/LBW infants to maintain temperature.
  • Monitor at-risk infants proactively.
  • Educate mothers on feeding cues and hypoglycemia signs.
SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS FOR SUDAN

• Human resource: Train nurses and midwives to recognize and manage hypoglycemia.
  • Equipment: Ensure glucometers and test strips are available; calibrate regularly.
  • Supply chain: Maintain stock of IV dextrose, feeding tubes, dextrose gel.
  • Community awareness: Integrate hypoglycemia education into antenatal and postnatal counseling.
  • Record keeping: Use simple bedside charts for glucose monitoring.
REFERENCES
UpToDate. Management and outcome of neonatal hypoglycemia. 2023.
Pediatric Endocrine Society. Guidelines for Evaluation and Management of Hypoglycemia in Neonates, Infants, and Children. 2015.
American Academy of Pediatrics. Postnatal Glucose Homeostasis in Late-Preterm and Term Infants. Pediatrics, 2011.
Rwanda Ministry of Health. National Neonatal Care Protocol, Third Edition, 2020.
WHO. Guidelines on Basic Newborn Resuscitation. 2012.

sections.title: Seizures: time targets and seizure or mimic

read.text: Critical Paradigms

• "Treat the EEG, Not Just the Baby" – 80% of neonatal seizures are electrographic-only.
  • "In neonatal neurology, time is measured in minutes, outcomes in lifetimes."
  • International Consortium on Neonatal Brain Protection, 2024
  • "Minutes Matter" – Seizure duration correlates with neuronal injury.
  • "Etiology Dictates Destiny" – Underlying cause determines 90% of outcome variance.
  • "Stop Before Discharge" – Acute provoked seizures rarely require chronic therapy.
Time-Sensitive Targets:

MilestoneTarget TimeQuality Indicator
Recognition → EEG initiation≤30 minutesGold standard
Seizure onset → 1st ASM dose≤10 minutesCritical
Complete etiologic workup≤2 hoursStandard
Seizure freedom≤60 minutesOptimal
RAPID DIAGNOSTIC PATHWAY
The 5-Minute Clinical Assessment
ESSENTIAL DIFFERENTIAL: Seizure vs. Mimic

FeatureSeizure (e.g., Focal Clonic)Non-Seizure Event (e.g., Jitteriness, Benign Myoclonus)
Stimulus SensitivityNot provoked by stimulus.Often provoked or enhanced by handling/stimulation.
Movement PatternRhythmic, slow (<4 jerks/sec), localized.Tremor-like, rapid, oscillatory, generalized.
Effect of RestraintPersists (you can feel the muscle contracting).Stops immediately with gentle restraint.
ConsciousnessOften altered.Normal (infant is awake or asleep but arousable).
Eye SignsMay have nystagmus or tonic deviation.Normal.
Seizure or mimic (jitteriness)? Sort each finding.

items.text: Not provoked by stimulus
Rhythmic, slow (< 4 jerks/sec), localised
Persists when you gently hold the limb
Stops immediately with gentle restraint
Tremor-like, rapid, generalised; baby awake, eyes normal

read.explanation: From the manual's table "Seizure vs. Mimic".

read.title: Neonatal seizure or jitteriness?
read.caption: Short clips of clonic, tonic and subtle seizures and of jitteriness, with the restraint test.

read.text: Step 1: Stabilization (ABCs)

• Airway & Breathing: Ensure patency, provide oxygen, prepare for ventilation if apneic.
  • Circulation: Secure IV/IO access, monitor heart rate and blood pressure.

sections.title: Seizures: finding the cause (SHOT) and the work-up

read.text: Step 2: Rapid Etiologic Evaluation ("SHOT" Mnemonic)

• S - Sugar & Sepsis:
    • Bedside Glucose: IMMEDIATELY check and treat hypoglycemia (<2.6 mmol/L or <45 mg/dL) with 10% Dextrose (2-5 mL/kg IV bolus, then maintenance infusion).
    • Infection Screen: Assume sepsis/meningitis until proven otherwise. Draw blood culture, start broad-spectrum antibiotics PLUS acyclovir (if HSV encephalitis is a possibility).
  • H - Hypoxia & History:
    • Assess for perinatal asphyxia (low Apgars, need for resuscitation). Consider Hypoxic-Ischemic Encephalopathy (HIE) as the leading cause.
    • Take a quick history: maternal fever, diabetes, drug use, difficult delivery, family history of neonatal seizures.
  • O - Osmolality & Electrolytes:
    • Check serum electrolytes, calcium, magnesium. Correct imbalances urgently.
    • Hypocalcemia: 10% Calcium Gluconate, 1-2 mL/kg (100-200 mg/kg) IV over 10 mins with cardiac monitoring.
    • Hypomagnesemia: 50% Magnesium Sulfate, 0.2 mL/kg (100 mg/kg) IM/IV slowly.
  • T - Trauma & Toxins/Treatable Metabolic:
    • Consider intracranial hemorrhage (especially in traumatic delivery).
    • Consider pyridoxine-dependent seizures in refractory cases. Empiric trial: Pyridoxine 100mg IV while monitoring EEG/respiration (risk of apnea).
In the SHOT mnemonic, what does the O stand for?
read.explanation: S: sugar and sepsis; H: hypoxia and history; O: osmolality and electrolytes; T: trauma, toxins and treatable metabolic causes.

read.text: Step 3: Systematic Diagnostic Workup

InvestigationPriority & RationaleResource-Adapted Note
Blood TestsGlucose, Electrolytes (Ca, Mg, Na), CBC, CRP, Blood Culture, Arterial Blood Gas.Minimum essential panel. Must be done for every infant.
Lumbar PunctureMandatory if infection is suspected. CSF for cell count, protein, glucose, culture, HSV PCR.Do not delay antibiotics for LP. Perform as soon as infant is stable.
Neuroimaging1. Cranial Ultrasound (Bedside): Excellent for detecting major IVH, hydrocephalus.
2. Brain MRI (Optimal): Gold standard for HIE patterns, stroke, malformations.		Ultrasound is a high-yield, accessible first step. MRI should be obtained when feasible for definitive diagnosis and prognosis.
EEG MonitoringcEEG is ideal. aEEG is a good screening alternative to guide therapy and detect subclinical (electrographic-only) seizures.If neither is available, treat based on strong clinical suspicion (focal clonic/tonic) and monitor clinical response closely.
Metabolic/GeneticConsider if initial workup is negative, seizures are refractory, or there is family history/consanguinity. Tests: ammonia, lactate, amino acids, urine organic acids, genetic epilepsy panel.Pyridoxine trial is a critical, low-cost therapeutic test. Collaboration with a referral center for advanced testing is key.
Neurodiagnostic Strategy
TIER 1: EEG MONITORING
Continuous video-EEG (cEEG) for:

• Therapeutic hypothermia
  • Unexplained encephalopathy
  • Clinical seizures
  • Paralysis/sedation
  • Screen: 24 hours minimum
• If seizures: Continue +24 hours after last seizure
• HIE: Throughout cooling + rewarming + 24h post
No EEG is available in your unit. A baby has focal clonic jerks. What does the manual say?
read.answer: If neither cEEG nor aEEG is available, treat based on strong clinical suspicion (focal clonic or tonic) and monitor the clinical response closely.

sections.title: Seizures: aEEG and neuroimaging

read.text: Amplitude-Integrated EEG (aEEG) when cEEG unavailable

• MUST include raw EEG tracing
  • Sensitivity 70-80% (shell-like, 2007)
  • Limitations: Misses focal, low-amplitude seizures
TIER 2: NEUROIMAGING
24 HOURS: Cranial ultrasound (bedside)
• Rule out hemorrhage/hydrocephalus
• Serial exams if abnormal
24-72 HOURS: MRI brain (when stable)
• 1.5T or 3T preferred
• Sequences: T1, T2, DWI, SWI, MRV
• Spectroscopy if metabolic disorder suspected
Which imaging is the accessible first step at the bedside, and what does it rule out?
read.explanation: Tier 2: cranial ultrasound at 24 hours (bedside); MRI at 24–72 hours when stable.

Should antibiotics wait until the lumbar puncture is done?
read.answer: No. The manual: "Do not delay antibiotics for LP. Perform as soon as infant is stable." The LP is mandatory if infection is suspected.

read.text: TREATMENT of Neonatal Seizer ALGORITHM
Phase 1: Immediate Intervention (0-15 minutes)

read.label: Standard operating procedure
read.text: Lumbar puncture · from the manual, Module 2, Section 7: Neonatal Procedures

• A. Indications
    • Lumbar puncture is used to confirm the diagnosis when the baby has signs suggestive of Meningitis.
Contraindications

• spina bifida/meningomylocele
  • Increased intracranial pressure (ICP):
  • Bleeding diathesis: Platelet count greater than 50,000/mm3 is desirable before LP, and correction of any clotting factor deficiencies can minimize the risk for bleeding and subsequent cord or nerve root compression.
  • Overlying skin infection may result in inoculation of CSF with organisms.
  • A mass or evidence of trauma to lumbar vertebrae
  • LP should be deferred in unstable patients, and appropriate therapy should be initiated, including antibiotics, if indicated.
Complications

• Local pain
  • apnea due to positioning
  • Bleeding
  • Infection
  • subarachnoid epidermal cyst
  • epidural CSF leak
  • spinal hematoma, and/or brainstem herniation
Supplies and material needed

• Sterile Gauze
  • Yamidine
  • Plaster
  • Spinal needle or intravenous needle (22- to 24-gauge)
  • Appropriate collection tubes
Preparation

• Be prepared to resuscitate the baby using a bag and mask, if necessary.
  • Place the baby under a radiant warmer, if possible, and undress the baby only when ready to perform the procedure.
  • Position the baby:
      • lateral recumbent position, with hips, knees, and neck flexed. Keep shoulders and hips aligned to avoid rotating the spine.
      • Have the assistant place one hand behind the baby’s head and neck, and place the other hand behind the baby’s thighs to hold the spine in a flexed position
      • Do not compromise a small infant’s cardiorespiratory status with positioning.
  • Locate the desired intervertebral space (either L3 to L4 or L4 to L5) by drawing an imaginary line between the top of the iliac crests. Alternatively, ultrasound can be used to mark the intervertebral space
  • Prepare the skin in a sterile fashion. Place sterile drapes over the baby’s body so that only the puncture site is exposed and .make monitoring the infant possible
  • Overlying skin and interspinous tissue can be anesthetized with 1% lidocaine or Apply local anesthetic cream if sufficient time is available.
PRACTISE THIS SKILL Procedure

• Insert the needle in the midline of the vertebrae, angled towards the baby’s umbilicus.
  • Slowly advance the needle several millimeters at a time, and withdraw stylet frequently to check for CSF flow. Needle may be advanced without the stylet once it is completely through the skin.
  • A slight “pop” may be felt as the needle enters the subarachnoid space. In small infants, one may not feel a change in resistance or “pop”
  • If resistance is met initially and the needle cannot be advanced, withdraw the needle to just under the skin surface and redirect the angle of the needle slightly upward while aiming for the baby’s umbilicus.
  • If CSF still does not come out, remove the needle and reinsert it between the fourth and fifth lumbar processes;
  • If blood is seen in the CSF, the needle probably went through the spinal canal and caused bleeding. If the CSF does not clear, collect enough CSF for culture and sensitivity only.
  • Send CSF for appropriate studies. In general, send the first tube for culture and Gram stain, the second tube for measurement of glucose and protein levels, and the last tube for cell count and differential.
  • After the CSF is collected, remove the needle. Have an assistant apply gentle pressure to the puncture site with a cotton wool ball until bleeding or leakage of fluid stops and apply an adhesive bandage to the site.
Where is a lumbar puncture done in a newborn?
options: L3–L4 or L4–L5, found on the line between the tops of the iliac crests
read.explanation: Baby in the lateral position with hips, knees and neck flexed, without compromising breathing. Tube 1 for culture and Gram stain, tube 2 glucose and protein, last tube cell count.

sections.title: Seizures: correct reversible causes first

read.text: STEP 1: Correct Reversible Causes FIRST
HYPOGLYCEMIA (<2.6 mmol/L):
• D10% 2 mL/kg IV bolus
• Start infusion 6-8 mg/kg/min
• Monitor glucose q1h until stable
HYPOCALCEMIA (ionized Ca <0.8 mmol/L):
• Calcium gluconate 10%: 1 mL/kg IV over 10 min
• CARDIAC MONITOR required
• Avoid extravasation (tissue necrosis risk)
HYPOMAGNESEMIA (<0.7 mmol/L):
• MgSO₄ 50%: 0.1 mL/kg IM or slow IV
• Often accompanies hypocalcemia
INFECTION SUSPECTED:
• Ampicillin 50 mg/kg IV + Gentamicin 5 mg/kg IV
• PLUS, Acyclovir 20 mg/kg IV q8h if HSV possible
• Meningitis doses if CSF suggestive

read.question: A 1.5 kg baby is seizing; ionised calcium is 0.7 mmol/L. What volume of 10% calcium gluconate (1 ml/kg) is given?
read.explanation: 1 ml/kg × 1.5 kg = 1.5 ml IV over 10 minutes, with a cardiac monitor, avoiding extravasation. Correct reversible causes first.

read.text: Why is the cause corrected before an antiseizure medicine is given?
options: A seizure with a correctable cause may stop once the cause is fixed
Because calcium works faster than any drug for every seizure
It is not: phenobarbital comes first
read.explanation: Step 1 of the treatment algorithm: "Correct reversible causes FIRST" (hypoglycaemia, hypocalcaemia, hypomagnesaemia, infection).

sections.title: Seizures: phenobarbital, the first-line medicine

read.text: STEP 2: First-Line Antiseizure Medication
PHENOBARBITAL (First-Line Recommendation):

• Loading: 20 mg/kg IV over 20 minutes
  • Therapeutic target: Serum 10-40 μg/mL
  • Maintenance dose: 3 to 5 mg/kg/day orally (PO) or IV every 12 hours; should be started 12 to 24 hours after the loading dose.
  • Monitor: Respiratory depression, hypotension
WHY PHENOBARBITAL:
• Superior to levetiracetam (80% vs 28% seizure freedom)
• Familiar safety profile
• IV/IM options available
ALTERNATIVE IF NO IV ACCESS:
• Phenobarbital IM (same dose) OR
• Midazolam 0.3 mg/kg buccal/nasal (monitor respiration)
Phase 2: Escalation (15-60 minutes)
IF SEIZURES PERSIST after 20 mg/kg Phenobarbital:

• 10 mg/kg IV in ten minutes may be given
  • Maximum loading: 40 mg/kg in first 24h
  • Check serum level if available (>40 μg/mL = toxicity risk)

read.question: What is the phenobarbital loading dose for a 3 kg baby (20 mg/kg)?
read.explanation: 20 mg/kg × 3 kg = 60 mg IV over 20 minutes. Monitor for respiratory depression and hypotension.

read.text: Seizures continue after the first 20 mg/kg of phenobarbital. What next?
options: A further 10 mg/kg IV over ten minutes, up to a maximum of 40 mg/kg in the first 24 hours
read.explanation: Phase 2: escalation (15–60 minutes). Check the serum level if available.

sections.title: Seizures: when they continue after 40 mg/kg phenobarbital

read.text: IF STILL SEIZING after 40 mg/kg Phenobarbital:
CHOOSE ONE based on availability/context:
OPTION A: LEVETIRACETAM

• LOAD: 20-40 mg/kg IV over 15 min
  • MAINTENANCE5-10 mg/kg/day every 12 hours; should be started 24 hours after loading dose. Maximum 60mg/kg
  • Preferred in cardiac/liver disease
OPTION B: FOSPHENYTOIN/PHENYTOIN

• 15- 20 mg/kg PE IV over 20 min (phenytoin equivalents)
  • Maintenance dose: 4 to 8 mg/kg/day every 8 hours
  • CARDIAC MONITOR mandatory
  • Avoid with lidocaine (arrhythmia risk)
  • First choice for suspected channelopathies
OPTION C: MIDAZOLAM INFUSION

• BOLUS: 0.15 mg/kg IV over 5 min
  • INFUSION: Start 0.06 mg/kg/hr, titrate to 0.4 mg/kg/hr max
  • PREPARE TO INTUBATE
  • Wean slowly after 24h seizure-free
OPTION D: LIDOCAINE INFUSION (Highly effective)

• LOAD: 2 mg/kg IV over 10 min
  • INFUSION: 6 mg/kg/hr × 4h → 3.5 × 12h → 1.75 × 12h
  • to be discontinued within 48 hours to avoid cardiotoxicity
  • keep serum lidocaine level below 9 mg/L
  • CONTRAINDICATIONS:
    • Congenital heart disease
    • Concurrent phenytoin
    • Hepatic impairment
Phase 3: Refractory Status Epilepticus (>60 minutes)
CONSIDER COMATOSE THERAPY:

• Midazolam infusion to burst-suppression on EEG
  • Consider thiopental/pentobarbital if available
  • ICU setting with ventilator support
METABOLIC TRIALS (CRITICAL STEP):
Perform sequential trials UNDER EEG MONITORING:

• Pyridoxine 100 mg IV q5min × 3 doses (max 500mg)
  • Pyridoxal-5'-phosphate 30 mg/kg/day if no B6 response
  • Biotin 10 mg IV
  • Folinic acid 2.5 mg IV
POSITIVE RESPONSE: EEG normalization within minutes
Seizures persist after 40 mg/kg of phenobarbital in a baby with congenital heart disease. Which option is contraindicated?
read.explanation: The manual lists contraindications to lidocaine: congenital heart disease, concurrent phenytoin, hepatic impairment. Levetiracetam is preferred in cardiac or liver disease.

read.text: Eye Care

Cord care: Proper care of the cord may prevent infection
