sections.title: Referring a newborn: why it must be organised

read.text: INTRODUCTION:
Neonatal transport is a critical phase of perinatal care, with specific needs for a specialized team and equipment to ensure maximal safety and efficiency.
Transferring a newborn from the labor room/ delivery facility to the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) involves a series of steps to ensure the baby's safety and well-being.
A simple, timely, efficient approach without any panic is required.
IMPORTANCE
Unplanned or non-organized newborn transfer from the labour room/ delivery facility to NICU may increase the mortality and morbidity leading to worse outcomes.
PROCESS OF TRANSPORT
The process of transferring a newborn to NICU can be arranged in the following steps

• Assessment and decision
  • Preparation before transfer
  • Communication
  • Transfer process.
Assessment and decision

As stated by NRP ‘Every delivery should be attended by at least one skilled health professional, such as a doctor, nurse, or midwife, who can provide essential medical care during labor and delivery, including identifying and managing potential complications’, the responsibility of the attending professional or team is to decide whether the newborn need further intensive care and admission to NICU.

In hospital settings a pediatrician or neonatologist assesses the newborn immediately after birth to determine if they need NICU care. However, if delivery was in a primary level of care or outside hospital, a trained health worker or midwife is responsible for the assessment.
Why does a newborn transfer need to be organised?
options: Unplanned or non-organised transfer may increase mortality and morbidity
Organised transfer is slower and less safe
It only matters for term babies
read.explanation: The manual: "Unplanned or non-organized newborn transfer ... may increase the mortality and morbidity leading to worse outcomes."

sections.title: Referring a newborn: assess, decide and stabilise

read.text: The attending health worker/midwife should carefully assess the baby to determine:

• vital signs
  • severity of distress
  • degree of maturity
  • presence of congenital anomalies or other complications
and consequently, decide for

• reason or indication for admission
  • level of care needed: this can be intensive care, HDU or SCBU.
  • type of respiratory support needed: such as nasal cannula, HHFNC, CPAP or ventilator.
Whenever possible the transport team shouldd communicate and discuss their assessment and decision to transfer the baby with the SCBU/NICU medical staff
Preparation before transfer
Once assessment done and decision to transfer the baby to NICU was taken, the team should work simultaneously to prepare for safe transport. By

• Stabilization
  • Checking equipment
  • Organizing team
  • Documentation
Stabilization
The assessment finding will lead the team to decide whether the baby is stable or needs to be stabilized before shifting. The team need to

• Maintain normal body temperature by treating and preventing hypothermia. This may involve increasing incubator temperature, covering, kangaroo care or use of plastic or polyethylene bags.
  • Maintain airway: head position or endotracheal tube stabilization
  • Maintain circulation: pulses, CRT. May need emergency vascular access and Providing fluids and nutrition (nasogastric feeds or intravenous fluids if unable to feed)
  • Giving antibiotics if indicated
  • Placing nasogastric tube for distended abdomen
  • Continue necessary support during transport.
A baby is to be transferred. Before moving, what does stabilisation include?
read.answer: Maintain normal body temperature (treat and prevent hypothermia), maintain the airway, maintain circulation (pulses, CRT, access, fluids or feeds), give antibiotics if indicated, place a nasogastric tube for a distended abdomen, and continue the necessary support during transport.

sections.title: Referring a newborn: equipment, team and documentation

read.text: Check equipment:
Transport equipment needs to be checked by assigned staff before moving.
This equipment may include

• oxygen source (cylinder or concentrator)
  • CPAP
  • T-piece
  • PPV bag
  • transport ventilator
  • transport incubator
  • monitors
  • infection control equipment.
Whenever a high risk delivery is anticipated and transfer of baby is expected, all equipment should be checked early and the transport incubator prewarmed.
The team leader should always confirm that equipment check was done and assure readiness for transport before moving.
Equipment failure during transport may lead to deterioration of the babyś situation and loss of valuable time.
Organizing transport team

• A qualified and experienced transport team should be assembled including nurses and medical staff or a trained community midwife.
  • A team leader decides the number of staff needed for transport, distributes the duties between members and supervises them.
  • A stable newborn may be transferred on a cot with a nurse. However, sick intubated preterm needs 2 or more medical and nursing staff.
  • Team duties would include preparation actions like assessing and taking decisions (usually by the most senior or team leader), stabilization and duties during transport like maintaining the airway or head position, ventilating or bagging, monitoring as well as maintaining safe transport.
Documentation
A team member should be assigned to document and record various steps of transport. These would include:

• Newborn data like GA, weight and diagnosis ABGAR Score at I, 5, and 10 min, Serial recording of vital signs and temperature before and after transfer,
  • equipment check, parental and staff communication, timing of moving to NICU and any event during transport.
Who should go with a sick, intubated preterm baby?
options: 2 or more medical and nursing staff

sections.title: Referring a newborn: communication

read.text: Communication

• Communication between neonatal unit and obstetric department or primary facility staff
  • Communication with parents
  • Communication with receiving team in NICU
  • Communication between team members.
  • Communication with ambulance for outborn cases.
Communication with parents: The parents are informed about the need for transfer and the reasons for it. The initial plan may be outlined if there is enough time.
Communication with NICU team: Establish clear communication channels, usually through phone call, between the transport team, and the receiving NICU.
The aim is to guide and assist the NICU team prepare and ensure its readiness to receive and welcome the baby.

The GA, diagnosis, level of care and type of respiratory support needed should be relayed clearly and should be re-read by the receiving team. E.g. ‘we are going to transfer an ex preterm, 28 weeks, RDS, intubated by size 3 ETT with stable vitals, to level 3 NICU for ventilatory support’

Communication between transport teams: The transport team should work in harmony. The orders or instructions by the team leader should be clear and address the specific team member, the team member should give clear feedback accordingly. E.G. ‘what is the baby’s temperature now, Ms. Mona’ ‘baby’s temperature now is 36.8-degree Dr’
Ensure that the ambulance is ready and equipped to transfer in the stated time.
Transfer process The aim is to achieve a
● Simple, comfortable
● Safe
● Stable
● Closely monitored transfer

options: The gestational age, diagnosis, level of care and type of respiratory support needed

read.text: Embrace portable warmer · from the manual, Module 2, Section 8: Equipment
Main Part

• Warm Pack: Contains a wax that melts at 37°C and releases heat as it solidifies, maintaining the baby's temperature for 4-6 hour.
  • Accu Temp Heater: A small electric heater to prepare the Warm Pack
  • Baby Wrap: contained for warm Pack and baby.
Standard Operating procedure

• 1. Wash hand and Ensure use clean disinfected BabyWrap
  • 2. Plug AccuTemp Heater to power source and put WarmPak inside heater for 30 minutes
  • 3. Once warm, place the warmed WarmPak inside a pouch in the BabyWrap
  • 4. Place the infant in the sleeping-bag-like garment BabyWrap
  • 5. Use the Rainbow sign to monitor target temperature.
  • 6. After use clean the BabyWrap and AccuTemp Heater.
Portable warmer Disinfection

• AccuTemp heater must be disinfect with appropriate solution (spirit or chlorine base solutions) before each use by wiping the devices surface.
  • WarmPak: has no direct contact with neonate. It should be cleaned whenever need by wipe using towel immerse in soap and water then wipe by appropriate disinfectant.
  • BabyWrap piece should be cleaned with soap and water between patient and patient
  • Use chlorine base solution 0.05% for 20 min only if there is blood then thoroughly wash in distil water and dry.

read.text: Kangaroo Fix Neonatal Restrain System

The baby is secured to its mother, ensuring that close contact is always maintained. The ‘face-up’ mode enables staff to monitor the baby, while the quick release system allows fast access. Maintains warmth. The system is lightweight and easy to store, as well as being easy to clean.
The most advanced method of transport currently is called transport shuttle which can be attached to an incubator or warmer and provides it with electrical power, oxygen supply and other equipment.
Whatever was the method available:

• 1. Each neonatal unit should use the most safe available method
  • 2. The delivery/ operation room and neonatal unit are preferably on the same level or there should be a safe access between them.
  • 3. Avoid delays and interruptions during transport.
  • 4. Keep monitoring and observing the baby during transport.
  • 5. Upon arrival, the baby is transferred to a SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU) bed and the team provides a detailed handover to the SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU) staff
Summary
Transferring a newborn is a complex process that needs to be safe and well organized.

• 1. Assess: vital signs, severity of distress, degree of maturity, presence of congenital anomalies or other complications
  • 2. Decide reason for admission, level of care needed, type of respiratory support needed.
  • 3. Stabilize and Maintain warmth A, B, Cs
  • 4. Check equipment: oxygen source (cylinder or concentrator), CPAP, T-piece, PPV bag, or transport ventilator, transport incubator, monitors and infection control equipment.
  • 5. Organize transport team and Assign duties
  • 6. Documentation: GA, weight and diagnosis. Serial recording of vital signs and temperature before and after transfer, equipment check, parental and staff communication, timing of moving to SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU) and any event during transport.
  • 7. Communication with parents, with SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU) team, between team members
  • 8. transfer
    • a. Inform SPECIAL CARE NEWBORN UNIT (SCNU) to anticipate time of arrival
    • b. use the safest available methods
    • c. Avoid delays and interruptions.
    • d. Keep monitoring and observing the baby during transport.
    • e. Upon arrival, provides a detailed handover to the special care newborn unit (SCNU) staff
Put the eight steps of transferring a newborn in order, then check.

exercises.source: Manual Module (1) Essential and Emergency Newborn Care, Section 2 exercises; answer key: Facilitator guide 2026
narrative: A 5-day-old newborn is brought into the emergency unit.
System Findings Weight 3 kg History Poor feeding, vomiting

questions.question: Q1. What is your assessment of this baby? Classify the problem. Q2. What are your immediate actions, in order of priority? Q3. What will you monitor, and when would you refer or escalate?
points: Question 1: What is your primary assessment?
Answer: Neonatal shock (cold type), complicated by respiratory distress and hypoglycaemia.
Question 2: What is your immediate and targeted management using the ABC approach?
Airway (A) & Breathing (B):
Secure the airway.
Administer oxygen to treat the hypoxaemia and respiratory distress.
Circulation (C):
Establish IV access immediately and draw labs (blood culture, metabolic panel).
Fluids: give normal saline or Ringer’s lactate.
– Calculation: 20 ml/kg × 3 kg = 60 ml. Give over 15 to 30 minutes. (Reduce to 10 ml/kg = 30 ml if cardiogenic shock is suspected.)
Antibiotics: give broad-spectrum empirical antibiotics immediately after drawing the cultures.
Support: prepare vasopressors (epinephrine or dopamine) if hypotension persists after the 60 ml fluid bolus.
Dextrose / Disability (D):
Treat the hypoglycaemia immediately to prevent further neurological deterioration.
Dextrose: give 10% dextrose (D10W).
– Calculation: 2 ml/kg × 3 kg = 6 ml IV bolus.
Question 3: What indicators show the baby is improving?
Normalized heart rate and blood pressure.
Stronger pulses, warm extremities, improved skin perfusion.
Improved alertness and return of normal reflexes — no longer lethargic.
Follow-up labs showing normal blood glucose, corrected metabolic acidosis, and reduced lactate.

Parameter Value Heart rate 180 / min Capillary refill time 5 seconds

questions.question: Q1. What is your assessment of this baby? Classify the problem. Q2. What are your immediate actions, in order of priority? Q3. What will you monitor, and when would you refer or escalate?
points: Expected Participant Responses
Signs of shock:
Tachycardia
Prolonged capillary refill
Cold extremities
Lethargy
Likely causes:
Sepsis
Hypovolaemia
Hypoglycaemia contributing Appropriate Actions
1. Immediate stabilization
Ensure airway and breathing are supported.
Keep the baby warm.
2. Correct hypoglycaemia
Give IV 10% dextrose bolus if indicated.
Start a glucose infusion.
3. Fluid management
Give a careful fluid bolus if there are signs of hypovolaemia: 10 ml/kg normal saline over 30–60 minutes.
Avoid rapid or repeated boluses without reassessment.
4. Start empirical antibiotics
As per the Sudan neonatal sepsis protocol.
Do NOT delay antibiotics waiting for labs.
5. Close monitoring
Reassess: heart rate, capillary refill, urine output, respiratory status.
6. Escalation
If no improvement: suspect septic shock, prepare for referral, consider inotropes where available.

exercises.source: Manual Module (1) Essential and Emergency Newborn Care, Section 2 exercises; answer key: Facilitator guide 2026
narrative: A premature newborn weighing 1.5 kg begins to exhibit clinical convulsions in the NICU.
Vitals & access: the infant has secure IV access and is currently stable on respiratory support.
Stat labs: a point-of-care test reveals an ionized calcium level of 0.7 mmol/L. Blood glucose and magnesium are normal.

questions.question: Q1. What is your assessment of this baby? Classify the problem. Q2. What are your immediate actions, in order of priority? Q3. What will you monitor, and when would you refer or escalate?
points: Facilitator Q&A Guide Task 1: Immediate intervention (0–15 minutes)
Question: According to Step 1 of the immediate intervention protocol, what is your first action based on the lab results?
Answer: You must correct the reversible cause first. The infant has hypocalcaemia (ionized Ca < 0.8 mmol/L). Action: treat immediately with 10% calcium gluconate IV.
Calculation: 1 ml/kg × 1.5 kg = 1.5 ml IV over 10 minutes, under cardiac monitoring. Avoid extravasation — tissue necrosis risk.
Task 2: First-line antiseizure medication
Question: The seizures continue despite correction of the calcium level. What is the first-line antiseizure medication, and what is the exact loading dose for this 1.5 kg infant?
Answer: The first-line medication is phenobarbital. The loading dose is 20 mg/kg IV over 20 minutes.
Calculation: 1.5 kg × 20 mg/kg = 30 mg IV.
Follow-up question: What side effects must you monitor for during this infusion?
Answer: Monitor closely for respiratory depression and hypotension.
Task 3: Phase 2 escalation (15–60 minutes)
Question: It has been 20 minutes since the phenobarbital loading dose was completed, but the infant is still seizing. What is your next immediate step?
Answer: Administer an additional dose of phenobarbital: 10 mg/kg IV over 10 minutes.
Calculation: 1.5 kg × 10 mg/kg = 15 mg IV.
Task 4: Further escalation (if seizures persist)
Question: The infant has now received a total of 40 mg/kg of phenobarbital in the first 24 hours (the maximum loading dose), but seizures persist. What are your pharmacological options now?

exercises.title: Sick & Small Newborn: SSN M1 · Case 2 — The Baby Who Was Never Seizing
exercises.source: Manual Module (1) Essential and Emergency Newborn Care, Section 2 exercises; answer key: Facilitator guide 2026 (line 2395)
narrative: A 2-day-old term baby, 3 kg, is referred for “fits”. The midwife describes shaking of both arms. On your examination the baby is awake, looking at you, and the arms are trembling rapidly. When you gently hold the wrist, the trembling stops. Blood glucose is 3.4 mmol/L. Temperature 36.9°C.
Ask the group:

questions.question: Q1. Apply STOP out loud. What do you find? Q2. Does this baby get phenobarbital? Q3. What would you tell the referring midwife?
points: This is jitteriness, not a seizure. S — provoked by handling. T — stops with gentle restraint. O — fast, tremor-like, generalized; eyes normal. P — the baby is awake and alert.
No phenobarbital. It would sedate a well baby and risk apnoea for nothing.
But still: check the glucose (done — normal), check the calcium, and ask about maternal drug use. Jitteriness is not always innocent — it just is not a seizure. Thank the midwife for referring.
She was right to be worried; the answer is teaching, not blame.
Teaching point: the commonest error in this session is not missing a seizure. It is treating a tremor. Both errors are dangerous — STOP protects you from the second one.
Checklist Neonatal Seizures
Rate each step: 2 = done correctly 1 = done incorrectly or incompletely 0 = not done NA = not applicable No. Step / Domain Performance Standard 2 1 0 NA 1.

1. Airway (A) & Breathing (B) Secures the airway and provides oxygen or ventilation as needed. Establishes continuous monitoring for respiratory depression. Recognizes that refractory cases may require an ICU setting with ventilator support 2.
2. Circulation (C) Promptly establishes IV access for medication delivery.
Monitors blood pressure closely to watch for hypotension 3.

Treat reversible causes Phase 1 (0–15 min): checks and corrects reversible causes FIRST — hypoglycaemia (< 2.6 mmol/L) with D10W IV; hypocalcaemia (ionized Ca < 0.8) with 10% calcium gluconate IV; hypomagnesaemia (< 0.7) with MgSO₄; empiric antibiotics and workup if infection suspected
4. Recognition Applies the STOP test and correctly distinguishes a true seizure from a mimic before giving any anticonvulsant
5. first-line meds
Administers phenobarbital: correctly calculates and gives a loading dose of 20 mg/kg IV over 20 minutes

6. escalation 1 Phase 2 (15–60 min): reassesses after the loading dose. If seizures persist, gives an additional 10 mg/kg IV over 10 minutes. Recognizes the maximum loading dose is 40 mg/kg in the first 24 h
7. escalation 2 If still seizing after 40 mg/kg, selects an appropriate second-line option: Levetiracetam · Fosphenytoin/phenytoin · Midazolam infusion · Lidocaine infusion

8. refractory Phase 3 (> 60 min): for refractory status epilepticus, escalates to comatose therapy (midazolam infusion to burst-suppression on EEG) or initiates critical metabolic trials (pyridoxine, pyridoxal-5′-phosphate, biotin, folinic acid) under EEG monitoring 9.
Reassessment / maintenance Plans maintenance dosing (phenobarbital 3–5 mg/kg/day PO or IV every 12 h, starting 12–24 h after loading) once seizures are controlled 10.
Documentation & referral Documents the seizure event on the standardized form; determines referral timing and prepares for safe transport
Final Evaluation: ☐ Competent (≥ 80 % ) ☐ Competent with supervision (60-79%) ☐ Not Competent (<60% )
6. Neonatal referral and transport Learning objectives
1. Identify type of transfer and babies who need referral.
2. Prepare and organize referral.
3. Provide counseling and family support.
4. Provide pre-referral stabilization and enroute care.
5. Documentation and handover.

Facilitator Script — Opening "unplanned or non-organized newborn transfer from the labour room or delivery facility to the NICU may increase mortality and morbidity, leading to worse outcomes. A simple, timely, efficient approach without any panic is required".

“An unstable baby who is moved will deteriorate on the way and may arrive in a moribund state — which defeats the whole purpose of the referral. The ambulance is not the treatment. What you do in the 30 minutes before the ambulance leaves is the treatment. Watch me do it, step by step.” Discussion what challenges facing neonatal transport Ask the group to mention challenges of neonatal transport, ensure they cover the following which of these they face: Write the group’s answers on the flip chart. Keep them visible — you will come back to them in the drill.
Facilities are scarce and not easily available.
Families have poor resources.
Organized transport services are not available — at times the baby may have to be transported on foot or by cart.
No health provider is available to accompany the baby.
Facilities are not fully geared up to receive sick neonates.
Communication systems are non-existent or inefficient.
Demonstration of transferee process

Facilitator: set up the manikin, transport incubator, oxygen cylinder, bag and mask, and monitoring equipment before the session. Run the demonstration in real time with a co-facilitator playing the team member. Participants observe first, then each group runs the sequence themselves.

"A baby needs to move. Watch what we do — and in what order. The order is not a suggestion. A baby who leaves before Step 3 is complete arrives worse than he left." Demonstrate each step, narrating as you go. Pause at Steps 3, 4 and 7 for the group to practise the specific skills below.
Step 1 — Assess The attending health worker or midwife carefully assesses the baby to determine:
Vital signs
Severity of distress
Degree of maturity
Presence of congenital anomalies or other complications “Make sure there is a genuine indication for referral. Do not move a baby because you are anxious.
Move a baby because the care they need is not here.” Step 2 — Decide
The reason or indication for admission.
The level of care needed — intensive care, HDU or SCBU.
The type of respiratory support needed — nasal cannula, HHFNC, CPAP or ventilator.
Whenever possible, the transport team communicates and discusses their assessment and decision with the SCBU/NICU medical staff before moving.
Step 3 — Stabilize (STABLE): Maintain Warmth, A, B, C It is of utmost importance that a neonate is stabilized before the transport is begun. Say this sentence out loud to the class.
Letter Assess Act Temperature By touch or thermometer Normalize BEFORE leaving. Warmer, KMC, plastic or polyethylene bag, cover, hat. Increase incubator temperature.
Airway Neck position, secretions in mouth/nose, chest movements Correct position with a shoulder roll. Suction.
Stabilize the ET tube if intubated.
Breathing Breathing effort, respiratory distress Tactile stimulation. Bag and mask with oxygen.
Oxygen supplementation as needed.

Circulation Pulse volume, capillary refill time If CRT > 3 sec and/or poor peripheral pulses with normal temperature: normal saline or Ringer lactate 10 ml/kg over 20–30 min. Reassess for further boluses. May need emergency vascular access.
Fluids Can the baby feed? If sick and unable to feed: maintenance fluid based on birth weight and day of life, plus any abnormal losses.
Medications Need for antibiotics, anticonvulsants, vitamin K Give before departure if indicated.
Feeding Suck, cup, gavage If the baby can be fed, feed enterally — breast, cup, or NG tube.
Also: place a nasogastric tube for a distended abdomen. Continue all necessary support during transport.
Step 4 — Check Equipment Transport equipment must be checked by assigned staff before moving:
Oxygen source (cylinder or concentrator)
CPAP
T-piece
PPV bag
Transport ventilator
Transport incubator
Monitors

Infection control equipment Whenever a high-risk delivery is anticipated and transfer is expected, all equipment should be checked early and the transport incubator prewarmed. The team leader must confirm that the equipment check was done and assure readiness before moving. Equipment failure during transport may lead to deterioration and loss of valuable time.
Oxygen — Do the Calculation Out Loud Portable oxygen needed = 2 × [FiO₂ flow (L/min) × expected journey time (minutes)]. A full transfer cylinder contains 250 L.

“The baby needs 2 litres a minute. The journey is 45 minutes. Two times two times forty-five is 180 litres. My cylinder holds 250. I have enough — but only just. What if we are delayed at a checkpoint? Take a second cylinder.” Step 5 — Organize the Team and Assign Duties
Assemble a qualified and experienced team — nurses and medical staff, or a trained community midwife.
A team leader decides the number of staff, distributes duties between members, and supervises them.
A stable newborn may be transferred on a cot with a nurse.
A sick intubated preterm needs 2 or more medical and nursing staff.

Duties include the preparation actions (assessing and deciding — usually by the most senior or the team leader, and stabilization) and the duties during transport: maintaining the airway or head position, ventilating or bagging, monitoring, and maintaining safe transport.
Step 6 — Documentation Assign one team member to document and record. This includes:
Newborn data: GA, weight, diagnosis
Apgar score at 1, 5 and 10 minutes
Serial recording of vital signs and temperature before and after transfer
The equipment check
Parental and staff communication
Timing of moving to the SCNU
Any event during transport Step 7 — Communication The manual lists five communication channels:
Between the neonatal unit and the obstetric department or primary facility staff
With the parents
With the receiving team in the NICU
Between team members
With the ambulance, for outborn cases
With the parents:
Explain the need for transfer and the reasons for it. Outline the initial plan if there is time.
Explain the condition and the prognosis.
Explain where to go and whom to contact.
Encourage the mother to accompany the baby.

With the receiving team: establish a clear channel, usually by phone. The GA, diagnosis, level of care and type of respiratory support needed should be relayed clearly and re-read back by the receiving team.
“We are going to transfer an ex-preterm, 28 weeks, RDS, intubated by size 3 ETT with stable vitals, to level 3 NICU for ventilatory support.”
Between team members: the team should work in harmony. Orders from the team leader must be clear and address a specific member by name; the member gives clear feedback.

“What is the baby’s temperature now, Ms. Mona?” — “Baby’s temperature now is 36.8 degrees, Doctor.” Demonstrate this exchange with a co-facilitator. Then have the whole class practise one closed-loop call-and-response before moving on.
Step 8 — Transfer
1. Inform the SCNU of the anticipated time of arrival.
2. Use the safest available method.
3. Avoid delays and interruptions.
4. Keep monitoring and observing the baby during transport.
5. On arrival, transfer the baby to an SCNU bed and give a detailed handover to the SCNU staff.
The aim is a transfer that is simple, comfortable, safe, stable and closely monitored.
Care During Transport Explain these to the accompanying person, whoever they are:
Element What to do No noxious stimuli Minimal handling. Reduce noise, light and painful procedures en route.
Emergent Stabilize and arrange for early referral — do not delay once the decision is made.
No sepsis Infection control practices during transport, with minimal handling.
Stabilize prior to transport The whole of Step 3 above. Never leave with an unstable baby.
Maintain the warm chain KMC · properly covered in cotton or cloth · improvised containers · transport incubator.
Prevent hypoglycaemia Breastfeed if the baby can suck. Cup-feed expressed breast milk if he can take cup feeds. For a long distance, insert a nasogastric catheter and give gavage feeding.
Maintain airway and breathing Neck in slight extension. Do NOT cover the baby's mouth and nose.
Gently wipe secretions with a cotton or cloth-covered finger. Watch the breathing — if the baby stops, stimulate the soles.
Educate the parents Teach them the danger signs to watch for during transport.
Case study – Transport Sick and small newborn
Purpose: the purpose of a clinical drill is to help participants practise responding to clinical situations that require immediate action.
How to Run It

Announce the case. The team has 10 minutes to prepare the baby and “leave”.

exercises.title: Sick & Small Newborn: SSN M1 · Case 1 — Temperature Problem
exercises.source: Manual Module (1) Essential and Emergency Newborn Care, Section 3 exercises; answer key: Facilitator guide 2026 (line 1719)
narrative: Baby Nour — female, born at term, 39 weeks gestation 90 minutes of age Baby Nour is 90 minutes old. She cried at birth and breastfed within the first hour. On examination she is active, breathing 44 breaths per minute with no chest indrawing, and pink. Her weight is 2900 g. Axillary temperature is 36.2°C.

questions.question: Q1. What is your assessment of this baby? Classify the problem. Q2. What are your immediate actions, in order of priority? Q3. What will you monitor, and when would you refer or escalate?
points: 36.2°C is not in the danger-sign row (Temp <35.5°C or >38°C) and not in the well-baby row (Temp 36.5–37.5°C).

It falls in the middle row: Weight 1500–<2500 g / Temp 35.5–38°C / Feeding difficulty / Risk of infection. Her weight (2900 g) is normal, but the temperature finding on its own places her in this row.
Apply the row's actions:
Maintain skin-to-skin, support breastfeeding, and treat risk of infection.
The “low weight or low temperature” sub-action applies: provide continuous skin-to-skin, improve thermal care.
Continue skin-to-skin contact; if interrupted, clothe/wrap in a clean, dry blanket and cover the head; avoid drafts and contact with wet or cold surfaces.

Reassess by touching the foot or forehead; if it feels too cool or too hot, measure with a thermometer. “if not improved or had danger sign, stabilize for referral” — “if improved, immunize and advise about home care.” Part B — one hour later
Read aloud to the provider:
“One hour later, Baby Nour's temperature is rechecked: 35.3°C. She is still skin-to-skin and attempting to breastfeed, but her feet feel cool to touch.”
1. Which row of the table applies now?
2. What must the provider do, in order?
Facilitator Answer Key — Part B
35.3°C is below 35.5°C — this now meets the top (danger-sign) row of the table. The action listed is: give antibiotics; stabilize for referral as needed.
Improve thermal care immediately: remove any wet clothing, cover the head, add a dry layer/blanket, warm the room, keep continuous, uninterrupted skin-to-skin contact.
Give antibiotics: give the first dose without delay, per the Sudan neonatal sepsis protocol (Ampicillin 50 mg/kg + Gentamicin 5 mg/kg). Do not delay waiting for investigations.

Stabilize for referral as needed: explain to the parents why urgent treatment and referral are needed; keep mother and baby together; maintain warmth and skin-to-skin during transport; complete a referral note.
Recheck temperature once thermal care is improved. Do not use uncontrolled heat sources — the manual warns against placing a baby close to heat sources and against over-wrapping.
Debrief questions:
Who in your facility is authorized to give the first antibiotic dose, and how quickly can this actually happen after a danger sign is identified?
What are the risks of overheating a baby while trying to correct hypothermia?

exercises.title: Sick & Small Newborn: SSN M1 · Case 2 — Birth Weight Problem
exercises.source: Manual Module (1) Essential and Emergency Newborn Care, Section 3 exercises; answer key: Facilitator guide 2026 (line 1770)
narrative: Baby Yasin — male, born at 32 weeks gestation Baby Yasin was born at 32 weeks gestation by spontaneous vaginal delivery at a health centre. He cried weakly at birth. At 90 minutes of age he is weighed: 1350 g. Temperature is 36.6°C. He is breathing 48 breaths per minute with no chest indrawing. He has not yet attempted to breastfeed.

questions.question: Q1. What is your assessment of this baby? Classify the problem. Q2. What are your immediate actions, in order of priority? Q3. What will you monitor, and when would you refer or escalate?
points: Weight <1500 g is listed on its own in the top row of the table — action: stabilize for referral as needed. This applies even though his temperature and breathing are currently normal. babies <1500 g “should receive advanced care and prolonged skin-to-skin (kangaroo mother care).”
Begin prolonged skin-to-skin (Kangaroo Mother) care with the mother or another family member.
Complete essential newborn care if not yet done: eye care, cord care, vitamin K.
Support attempts at the breast; if he cannot attach, plan for expressed breast milk by cup or tube, per the table's feeding-difficulty sub-action.
Prepare for referral if this facility cannot provide the advanced care,Complete the newborn record and fill a referral note; keep mother and baby together.

exercises.title: Sick & Small Newborn: SSN M1 · Case 3 — Feeding Problem
exercises.source: Manual Module (1) Essential and Emergency Newborn Care, Section 3 exercises; answer key: Facilitator guide 2026 (line 1794)
narrative: Baby Salma — female, born at 35 weeks gestation Baby Salma is 4 hours old, born at 35 weeks, weighing 1950 g. Temperature is 36.8°C and breathing is normal. She attempted to breastfeed at 1 hour of age but has not latched. She licks at the nipple but falls asleep after a few minutes without sucking.

questions.question: Q1. What is your assessment of this baby? Classify the problem. Q2. What are your immediate actions, in order of priority? Q3. What will you monitor, and when would you refer or escalate?
points: Weight 1950 g (1500–<2500 g) with feeding difficulty places her in the table's middle row.
The row's feeding-difficulty sub-action lists:

Support attachment keep mother and baby together; encourage breastfeeding whenever she shows signs of readiness; help the mother into a comfortable, semi-reclined position, baby held close, supported along the whole body, head and body in line, facing the breast.
Express breast milk and feed with cup or tube, exactly as the table's sub-action states.
Reassess using signs of good attachment: more areola seen above the lips than below; mouth wide open; lower lip turned outward; chin touching the breast.
If not improved, or a danger sign appears, stabilize for referral

narrative: Baby Mohammed — male, born at 33 weeks gestation 90 minutes of age Baby Mohammed was born at 33 weeks by vaginal delivery, birth weight 2700 g. At 90 minutes of age his temperature is 36.7°C, breathing is 40 breaths per minute with no chest indrawing, and he well attached to the breast.

points: Weight 2700 g, temperature 36.7°C, and feeding well all sit inside the table's lower row. lower- row actions:
Maintain normal temperature
Support breastfeeding
Advise about breastfeeding problems
Reassess for discharge
Immunize
Advise about home care

5. Selected Neonatal Emergencies Introduction This section focuses on time-critical neonatal emergencies that commonly cause preventable death or brain injury in Sudan if recognition or treatment is delayed.
Core principle to emphasize:
Recognize early → Treat immediately → Reassess → Refer if needed LEARNING OBJECTIVES By the end of this section, participants should be able to:
Knowledge
Identify early and late signs of neonatal shock
Define neonatal hypoglycemia and seizure emergencies
Describe first-line emergency management Skills
Perform rapid emergency assessment
Initiate correct immediate treatment
Stabilize newborns prior to referral Attitudes
Act without delay
Prioritize safety and reassessment
Communicate clearly with the team and family

narrative: A baby born at 28 weeks, 1.1 kg, in a facility with no ventilator. Grunting, chest indrawing, SpO₂ 84% on nasal cannula. Temperature 35.8°C. The nearest level 3 NICU is 45 minutes away.
Ask the team:

questions.question: Q1. Is there a genuine indication for referral? What level of care and what respiratory support? Q2. What must be corrected before you leave? Q3. How much oxygen do you need for the journey? Q4. Who accompanies the baby?
points: airway; consider elective intubation if in doubt. Check glucose. Calculate oxygen: 2 × (flow × 45). Sick preterm needs 2 or more staff. Phone the NICU with a clear read-back handover.
Document the temperature before and after.
